# Overview



**AlphaFold 3** is DeepMind's third-generation protein structure prediction system — a quantum leap beyond its predecessors. Where AlphaFold 2 predicted single-chain and multimer protein structures, AlphaFold 3 extends its reach to **biomolecular interactions** across the entire structural biology landscape: proteins, RNA, DNA, small molecule ligands, post-translational modifications, and covalent bonds between entities. This is the inference pipeline implementation, licensed under Apache 2.0 with model parameters governed by separate terms of use.

![header](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/blob/main/docs/header.jpg?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L25), [src/alphafold3/__init__.py](/src/alphafold3/__init__.py#L20-L21)

## What AlphaFold 3 Predicts

AlphaFold 3 models the **3D atomic structure** of biomolecular complexes from sequence information alone. The system accepts a JSON input describing one or more chains and ligands, runs a genetic and structural database search pipeline, feeds the resulting features through a deep neural network, and outputs atomic coordinates in mmCIF format alongside per-residue and per-atom confidence metrics.

| Entity Type | Input Specification | Capability |
|---|---|---|
| **Protein** | Amino acid sequence + optional modifications | Full atomistic prediction, MSA + template search |
| **RNA** | Nucleotide sequence + optional modifications | MSA search via Nhmmer against NT-RNA / Rfam / RNAcentral |
| **DNA** | Nucleotide sequence + optional modifications | Structure prediction without MSA search |
| **Ligand (CCD)** | Chemical Component Dictionary code | 3D conformer from CCD or RDKit generation |
| **Ligand (SMILES)** | SMILES string | RDKit conformer generation |
| **Covalent bonds** | Bond definitions between entities | Inter-chain and intra-chain covalent linking |

Sources: [docs/input.md](/docs/input.md#L29-L41), [src/alphafold3/common/folding_input.py](/src/alphafold3/common/folding_input.py#L43-L51)

## Architecture at a Glance

AlphaFold 3 operates as a **two-stage pipeline** that can be independently controlled: a CPU-bound **data pipeline** (MSA + template search) and a GPU-bound **inference pipeline** (neural network forward pass + post-processing). The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow from input JSON to output structure.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input
        JSON["Input JSON<br/>(protein/RNA/DNA/ligand)"]
    end

    subgraph DataPipeline["Data Pipeline (CPU)"]
        MSA["MSA Search<br/>Jackhmmer / Nhmmer"]
        PAIR["MSA Pairing<br/>(multimer)"]
        TMPL["Template Search<br/>Hmmsearch → PDB"]
        FEAT["Featurisation &<br/>Batch Assembly"]
    end

    subgraph NeuralNetwork["Neural Network (GPU)"]
        EVO["Evoformer Trunk<br/>48 Pairformer layers"]
        DIFF["Diffusion Module<br/>Atom-level denoising"]
        CONF["Confidence Head<br/>pLDDT / PAE / pTM"]
    end

    subgraph Output
        CIF["mmCIF Structure<br/>+ Confidence JSON"]
    end

    JSON --> MSA
    MSA --> PAIR
    MSA --> TMPL
    PAIR --> FEAT
    TMPL --> FEAT
    FEAT --> EVO
    EVO --> DIFF
    EVO --> CONF
    DIFF --> CIF
    CONF --> CIF
```

Sources: [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L48-L59), [src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py](/src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L20-L36), [src/alphafold3/model/model.py](/src/alphafold3/model/model.py#L38-L47)

## Project Structure

The codebase is organized as a Python package (`alphafold3`) with C++ extensions for performance-critical components (MSA profiles, JSON serialization, DSSP, structure parsing). The entry point is `run_alphafold.py` at the repository root.

```
alphafold3/
├── run_alphafold.py              # Main entry point — orchestrates both pipelines
├── src/alphafold3/
│   ├── common/                   # Shared types: FoldingInput, BaseConfig, Resources
│   ├── constants/                # Chemical constants: atom types, residue names, periodic table
│   ├── data/                     # Data pipeline: MSA search, templates, featurisation
│   │   ├── pipeline.py           #   → Orchestrates MSA + template tools
│   │   ├── featurisation.py      #   → Converts raw data → model features
│   │   ├── tools/                #   → Jackhmmer, Nhmmer, Hmmsearch wrappers
│   │   └── cpp/                  #   → C++ MSA profile computation
│   ├── model/                    # Neural network: inference core
│   │   ├── network/              #   → Evoformer, DiffusionHead, ConfidenceHead, AtomCrossAttention
│   │   ├── pipeline/             #   → Model featurizer & structure cleaning
│   │   ├── scoring/              #   → Alignment, chirality, ranking scores
│   │   └── model.py              #   → Top-level model class & InferenceResult
│   ├── jax/geometry/             # JAX-based rigid body geometry operations
│   ├── structure/                # Structure I/O: mmCIF parsing, bonds, bioassemblies
│   └── parsers/                  # C++ accelerated bioinformatics parsers
├── examples/                     # 13 sample input JSON files
├── docker/                       # Dockerfile + jackhmmer patch
└── docs/                         # Official documentation
```

Sources: [src/alphafold3/](/src/alphafold3/__init__.py#L20-L21), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L48-L66)

## Neural Network Core

The model architecture represents a fundamental redesign from AlphaFold 2. Three key innovations define the AlphaFold 3 network:

**Evoformer Trunk** — The backbone processing module takes MSA, pair, and single embeddings through 48 Pairformer layers (replacing the separate MSA + pair streams of AF2). It integrates template embeddings and per-atom cross-attention conditioning to produce refined single and pair representations. Channel dimensions are `seq_channel=384` and `pair_channel=128`.

**Diffusion Module** — AlphaFold 3 replaces AF2's structure module with a **diffusion-based atom-level decoder**. Instead of predicting an SE(3) frame per residue, it directly predicts all atom positions through iterative denoising. The `SIGMA_DATA=16.0` constant governs the noise schedule, calibrated against the multimer training set. Multiple diffusion samples (default: 5) are generated per seed, and the top-ranking prediction is selected.

**Confidence Head** — A lightweight 4-layer Pairformer predicts per-token pLDDT scores, predicted aligned error (PAE), and predicted TM-score (pTM). These metrics guide the ranking of multiple sampled predictions.

| Component | Key Parameter | Default Value |
|---|---|---|
| Pairformer layers | `num_layer` | 48 |
| Sequence channel | `seq_channel` | 384 |
| Pair channel | `pair_channel` | 128 |
| MSA channel | `msa_channel` | 64 |
| Diffusion samples | `num_diffusion_samples` | 5 |
| Recycles | `num_recycles` | 10 |
| Confidence Pairformer layers | `num_layer` | 4 |

> [!TIP]
> The data pipeline (`--run_data_pipeline`) is CPU-only and can be run separately from inference (`--run_inference`), which requires a GPU. Decoupling these stages is essential for resource-efficient batch processing.

Sources: [src/alphafold3/model/network/evoformer.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/evoformer.py#L39-L74), [src/alphafold3/model/network/diffusion_head.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/diffusion_head.py#L38-L39), [src/alphafold3/model/network/confidence_head.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/confidence_head.py#L38-L60), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L379-L389)

## Runtime Requirements

AlphaFold 3 has significant hardware demands driven by the size of the genetic databases (~1 TB) and the GPU memory requirements for inference on large complexes.

| Requirement | Specification |
|---|---|
| **Operating System** | Linux only |
| **GPU** | NVIDIA Compute Capability ≥ 8.0 (Ampere+) |
| **Verified GPUs** | A100 80 GB, H100 80 GB |
| **Max tokens on A100/H100** | 5,120 tokens |
| **RAM** | ≥ 64 GB (for long targets during genetic search) |
| **Disk** | ~1 TB SSD recommended (for databases) |
| **CUDA** | 12.6 (Docker host requirement) |
| **Python** | ≥ 3.12 |

> [!TIP]
> Token count is the primary scaling dimension. A token corresponds to one amino acid/nucleotide or one ligand entity. Inputs exceeding 5,120 tokens require GPUs with more than 80 GB VRAM or model parallelism.

Sources: [docs/installation.md](/docs/installation.md#L1-L13), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L14-L29), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L356-L365)

## Key Dependencies

The implementation leverages several specialized libraries for its computational backbone:

| Library | Role |
|---|---|
| **JAX** (0.10.2) | Differentiable computing framework — all neural network ops |
| **Haiku** (0.0.17) | JAX-native neural network library (module abstractions) |
| **Tokamax** (0.0.12) | Flash attention implementations (Triton/cuDNN/XLA) |
| **RDKit** (2025.9.4) | Small molecule conformer generation, SMILES parsing |
| **HMMER Suite** | Jackhmmer (protein MSA), Nhmmer (RNA MSA), Hmmsearch (templates) |
| **DSSP** | Secondary structure assignment from predicted coordinates |
| **pybind11** | C++ ↔ Python bindings for performance-critical parsers |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L17-L29), [README.md](/README.md#L137-L152)

## Input → Output at a Glance

**Input** is a JSON file specifying chains, ligands, bonds, and model seeds. The format supports both the native `alphafold3` dialect (more features) and the `alphafoldserver` dialect (auto-converted). Thirteen example input files cover common scenarios — protein-protein complexes, protein-ligand binding, RNA-protein interactions, glycosylated proteins, and modified DNA/RNA.

**Output** is a directory containing per-sample mmCIF files with predicted atomic coordinates, per-sample confidence JSONs, a top-ranking prediction symlink, and a `ranking_scores.csv` summarizing all samples. Embeddings and distograms can optionally be saved.

Sources: [docs/input.md](/docs/input.md#L1-L15), [docs/output.md](/docs/output.md#L1-L46), [examples/barnase_barstar.json](/examples/barnase_barstar.json#L1-L22)

## License & Model Parameters

The source code is under **Apache License 2.0**, but the model parameters are governed by separate [Terms of Use](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/blob/main/WEIGHTS_TERMS_OF_USE.md). Parameters may only be used if received directly from Google (downloadable from `gs://alphafold3/af3.bin.zst`). Outputs are predictions with varying confidence and are **not intended for clinical use**.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L171-L200), [WEIGHTS_TERMS_OF_USE.md](/WEIGHTS_TERMS_OF_USE.md#L1-L1)

# Quick Start



Get AlphaFold 3 running from zero to your first structure prediction. This guide walks you through the complete setup pipeline — from provisioning a GPU machine to producing your first predicted biomolecular structure — using the official Docker-based workflow.

## Prerequisites at a Glance

AlphaFold 3 has specific hardware and software requirements. Before starting, confirm your environment meets these thresholds:

| Requirement | Specification | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Operating System** | Linux | macOS supported in CPU-only / MPS mode only |
| **GPU** | NVIDIA with Compute Capability ≥ 8.0 | A100 80 GB and H100 80 GB are verified |
| **GPU Memory** | 80 GB recommended | Larger memory → larger predictions (up to 5,120 tokens on 80 GB) |
| **System RAM** | ≥ 64 GB | Genetic search for long targets can consume significant RAM |
| **Disk Space** | ~1 TB | ~630 GB for databases (uncompressed) + model params + working space |
| **Storage Type** | SSD recommended | Critical for genetic search I/O performance |
| **CUDA (host)** | 12.6 | Required by the Docker container |

> [!TIP]
> Inputs with up to 5,120 tokens have been verified on a single NVIDIA A100 80 GB or H100 80 GB. The `--num_recycles` and `--num_diffusion_samples` flags control inference depth vs. speed trade-offs.

Sources: [installation.md](docs/installation.md#L3-L9), [performance.md](docs/performance.md#L186-L200)

## Setup Flow

The end-to-end setup follows six sequential stages, each producing an artifact consumed by the next:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["1. Install Docker &<br/>NVIDIA Toolkit"] --> B["2. Clone Repository"]
    B --> C["3. Fetch Genetic Databases<br/>(~252 GB download)"]
    C --> D["4. Download Model Parameters<br/>(af3.bin.zst)"]
    D --> E["5. Build Docker Image"]
    E --> F["6. Run Prediction"]

    style A fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4285f4
    style B fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4285f4
    style C fill:#fef7e0,stroke:#f9ab00
    style D fill:#fef7e0,stroke:#f9ab00
    style E fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4285f4
    style F fill:#e6f4ea,stroke:#34a853
```

Sources: [installation.md](docs/installation.md#L23-L31), [Dockerfile](docker/Dockerfile#L20-L98)

## Step 1 — Install Docker and GPU Support

AlphaFold 3 runs inside a Docker container with GPU passthrough. Install rootless Docker and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit on your Ubuntu 22.04 LTS host:

```sh
# Install Docker
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
echo \
  "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu \
  $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable" | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin

# Enable rootless Docker (see docs for full instructions)
sudo apt-get install -y uidmap systemd-container
```

Then install NVIDIA drivers and the container toolkit:

```sh
# NVIDIA drivers
sudo apt-get -y install alsa-utils ubuntu-drivers-common
sudo ubuntu-drivers install
nvidia-smi  # Verify — reboot if this fails

# NVIDIA Container Toolkit
curl -fsSL https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg \
  && curl -s -L https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/nvidia-container-toolkit.list | \
    sed 's#deb https://#deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg] https://#g' | \
    sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-container-toolkit
nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker --config=$HOME/.config/docker/daemon.json
systemctl --user restart docker
sudo nvidia-ctk config --set nvidia-container-cli.no-cgroups --in-place
```

**Verify GPU access from Docker** before proceeding:

```sh
docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.6.0-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi
```

Sources: [installation.md](docs/installation.md#L61-L156)

## Step 2 — Clone the Repository

```sh
git clone https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3.git
cd alphafold3
```

Sources: [installation.md](docs/installation.md#L185-L189)

## Step 3 — Fetch Genetic Databases

AlphaFold 3 requires multiple genetic databases for MSA and template search. The provided `fetch_databases.sh` script downloads all of them in parallel:

```sh
./fetch_databases.sh [<DB_DIR>]
```

If `<DB_DIR>` is not specified, it defaults to `$HOME/public_databases`. This step downloads approximately **252 GB** and decompresses to approximately **630 GB** — expect around 45 minutes on a non-SSD connection. Run this in a `screen` or `tmux` session.

The resulting directory structure:

```
<DB_DIR>/
├── mmcif_files/                                                # ~200k PDB mmCIF files
├── bfd-first_non_consensus_sequences.fasta                    # BFD small
├── mgy_clusters_2022_05.fa                                    # MGnify
├── nt_rna_2023_02_23_clust_seq_id_90_cov_80_rep_seq.fasta     # NT RNA
├── pdb_seqres_2022_09_28.fasta                                # PDB seqres
├── rfam_14_9_clust_seq_id_90_cov_80_rep_seq.fasta             # RFam
├── rnacentral_active_seq_id_90_cov_80_linclust.fasta          # RNAcentral
├── uniprot_all_2021_04.fa                                     # UniProt
└── uniref90_2022_05.fa                                        # UniRef90
```

> [!TIP]
> **Do not** place `<DB_DIR>` inside the AlphaFold 3 repository directory — Docker will copy it during the image build, making it extremely slow. Also ensure full read/write permissions: `sudo chmod 755 --recursive <DB_DIR>`.

Sources: [fetch_databases.sh](fetch_databases.sh#L21-L57), [installation.md](docs/installation.md#L192-L250)

## Step 4 — Download Model Parameters

Fetch the model weights from Google Cloud Storage:

```sh
wget https://storage.googleapis.com/alphafold3/af3.bin.zst
```

Place the downloaded file in a directory referred to as `<MODEL_PARAMETERS_DIR>`. As with databases, this directory **must not** be a subdirectory of the AlphaFold 3 repository. Use of these parameters is subject to the [AlphaFold 3 Model Parameters Terms of Use](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/blob/main/WEIGHTS_TERMS_OF_USE.md).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L27-L32), [installation.md](docs/installation.md#L265-L274)

## Step 5 — Build the Docker Image

From the root of the cloned repository:

```sh
docker build -t alphafold3 -f docker/Dockerfile .
```

On systems like AlmaLinux/Rocky/RHEL that hit `No file descriptors available (os error 24)`, expand the limit:

```sh
docker build --ulimit nofile=65535:65535 -t alphafold3 -f docker/Dockerfile .
```

The Dockerfile builds on `nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-base-ubuntu24.04`, installs HMMER 3.4 (with a custom sequence limit patch), sets up a Python 3.12 virtual environment via `uv`, and configures XLA flags for optimal GPU compilation. The build also pre-compiles the chemical components database (`build_data`).

Sources: [Dockerfile](docker/Dockerfile#L20-L98), [installation.md](docs/installation.md#L275-L290)

## Step 6 — Run Your First Prediction

### Prepare Your Input JSON

Create an input file `fold_input.json` describing the structure you want to predict. Here is a minimal protein homodimer example:

```json
{
  "name": "2PV7",
  "sequences": [
    {
      "protein": {
        "id": ["A", "B"],
        "sequence": "GMRESYANENQFGFKTINSDIHKIVIVGGYGKLGGLFARYLRASGYPISILDREDWAVAESILANADVVIVSVPINLTLETIERLKPYLTENMLLADLTSVKREPLAKMLEVHTGAVLGLHPMFGADIASMAKQVVVRCDGRFPERYEWLLEQIQIWGAKIYQTNATEHDHNMTYIQALRHFSTFANGLHLSKQPINLANLLALSSPIYRLELAMIGRLFAQDAELYADIIMDKSENLAVIETLKQTYDEALTFFENNDRQGFIDAFHKVRDWFGDYSE"
      }
    }
  ],
  "modelSeeds": [1],
  "dialect": "alphafold3",
  "version": 1
}
```

Place it in a directory, e.g. `$HOME/af_input`. The repository includes **13 ready-made example inputs** in the `examples/` directory covering proteins, RNA, DNA, ligands (by CCD code and SMILES), modified residues, covalent bonds, and glycosylated chains.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L38-L56), [input.md](docs/input.md#L116-L136)

### Execute the Prediction

```sh
docker run -it \
    --volume $HOME/af_input:/root/af_input \
    --volume $HOME/af_output:/root/af_output \
    --volume <MODEL_PARAMETERS_DIR>:/root/models \
    --volume <DB_DIR>:/root/public_databases \
    --gpus all \
    alphafold3 \
    python run_alphafold.py \
    --json_path=/root/af_input/fold_input.json \
    --model_dir=/root/models \
    --output_dir=/root/af_output
```

The four `--volume` flags map host directories into the container: input JSON, output directory, model parameters, and genetic databases. Ensure `$HOME/af_output` exists and is writable (`chmod 755 $HOME/af_output`).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L60-L72), [installation.md](docs/installation.md#L298-L318)

### What You'll Get

After the run completes, the output directory contains your predicted structure and confidence metrics:

```
2PV7/
├── seed-1_sample-0/
│   ├── 2PV7_seed-1_sample-0_model.cif          # Predicted structure (mmCIF)
│   ├── 2PV7_seed-1_sample-0_confidences.json   # Full confidence arrays
│   └── 2PV7_seed-1_sample-0_summary_confidences.json
├── seed-1_sample-1/
│   └── ...
├── 2PV7_model.cif                               # Top-ranking prediction
├── 2PV7_confidences.json                         # Top-ranking confidences
├── 2PV7_summary_confidences.json                 # Summary (pTM, ipTM, ranking_score)
├── 2PV7_data.json                                # Input + MSA/template data
├── 2PV7_ranking_scores.csv                       # All samples ranked
└── TERMS_OF_USE.md
```

By default, AlphaFold 3 generates **5 diffusion samples per seed**. The top-ranked sample (by `ranking_score`) is promoted to the root directory. The primary mmCIF file is compatible with standard structural biology tools.

Sources: [output.md](docs/output.md#L1-L83)

## Key Command-Line Flags

The `run_alphafold.py` script exposes many flags for controlling behavior. Discover all options with `docker run alphafold3 python run_alphafold.py --help`. The most important ones for getting started:

| Flag | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `--json_path` | *(required)* | Path to input JSON file |
| `--model_dir` | `~/models` | Path to model parameters directory |
| `--output_dir` | *(required)* | Path to output directory |
| `--run_data_pipeline` | `true` | Run MSA + template search (CPU-only stage) |
| `--run_inference` | `true` | Run model inference (requires GPU) |
| `--jax_backend` | `gpu` | JAX backend: `gpu`, `cpu`, or `mps` (Apple Silicon) |
| `--num_recycles` | `10` | Number of recycles during inference |
| `--num_diffusion_samples` | `5` | Number of diffusion samples per seed |
| `--max_template_date` | `2021-09-30` | Ignore templates released after this date |
| `--flash_attention_implementation` | `triton` | Attention kernel: `triton` (fastest), `cudnn`, or `xla` (portable) |

The `--run_data_pipeline` and `--run_inference` flags are especially powerful when used independently — you can run the CPU-intensive data pipeline on a machine without a GPU, then transfer the augmented JSON to a GPU machine for inference only. See [Performance Optimization](21-performance-optimization) for advanced staging strategies.

Sources: [run_alphafold.py](run_alphafold.py#L80-L111), [run_alphafold.py](run_alphafold.py#L344-L390), [README.md](README.md#L74-L82)

## Example Input Gallery

The `examples/` directory provides 13 input JSON files spanning the full range of AlphaFold 3's capabilities. Use these as templates for your own inputs:

| Example File | Entity Types | Key Feature Demonstrated |
|---|---|---|
| `ubiquitin_monomer.json` | Protein | Simple single-chain protein |
| `barnase_barstar.json` | Protein + Protein | Protein–protein complex |
| `tetr_homodimer.json` | Protein | Symmetric homodimer |
| `modified_rna.json` | RNA (modified) | Pseudouridine, methylcytidine, O-methylguanosine |
| `u1a_rna_hairpin.json` | Protein + RNA | Protein–RNA interaction |
| `tetr_dimer_dna.json` | Protein + DNA | Protein–DNA interaction |
| `methylated_dna.json` | DNA (modified) | Methylated DNA bases |
| `kras_g12c_sotorasib.json` | Protein + Ligand (CCD) | Covalent bond (`bondedAtomPairs`) |
| `streptavidin_biotin_smiles.json` | Protein + Ligand (SMILES) | Ligand specified by SMILES string |
| `rnaseb_glycosylated.json` | Protein (glycosylated) | N-linked glycosylation |
| `calmodulin_4calcium.json` | Protein + Ions | Calcium ions as ligand entities |
| `erk2_phosphorylated.json` | Protein (phosphorylated) | Phosphorylated residues |
| `tetr_dimer_tetracycline.json` | Protein + Ligand (CCD) | Small-molecule binding |

Sources: [examples/](examples/), [input.md](docs/input.md#L27-L45)

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `nvidia-smi` fails after driver install | GPU needs reset | Run `sudo reboot now` |
| Docker container cannot see GPU | NVIDIA toolkit not configured | Verify with `docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.6.0-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi` |
| `permission denied` on volume mounts | Host directory permissions | `chmod 755 $HOME/af_input $HOME/af_output` |
| Slow genetic search | Databases on HDD, not SSD | Move databases to SSD and mount separately |
| `No file descriptors available` during build | OS file descriptor limits | Add `--ulimit nofile=65535:65535` to `docker build` |
| Opaque MSA tool errors | Database directory lacks read/write permissions | `sudo chmod 755 --recursive <DB_DIR>` |

For additional known issues, see [Issues and Feedbacks](5-issues-and-feedbacks).

Sources: [installation.md](docs/installation.md#L119-L132), [installation.md](docs/installation.md#L223-L236), [installation.md](docs/installation.md#L284-L289)

- **[Input Examples and Patterns](22-input-examples-and-patterns)** — Detailed walkthroughs of all 13 example inputs

# Input JSON Format



AlphaFold 3 accepts a **custom JSON input format** that provides fine-grained control over every molecular entity in your prediction — from protein chains with post-translational modifications to covalently bonded ligands defined via SMILES or the Chemical Component Dictionary (CCD). This page is your definitive reference for constructing valid input JSONs, understanding every field, and avoiding common pitfalls like SMILES escaping, MSA pairing semantics, and template index offsets.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L1-L1056), [run_alphafold.py](run_alphafold.py#L1-L200)

## Specifying Input to `run_alphafold.py`

You provide inputs via one of two CLI flags:

| Flag | Behavior | Path Type |
|---|---|---|
| `--json_path <file>` | Process a single JSON file | Local path or `gs://` GCS path |
| `--input_dir <dir>` | Process every JSON file in a directory | Local dir or `gs://` GCS path |

Within any input JSON, fields ending in `Path` (e.g. `pairedMsaPath`, `userCCDPath`) also accept GCS paths if the optional `gcsfs` dependency is installed. Paths in `*Path` fields may be **absolute** or **relative to the input JSON file's location**.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L5-L18), [run_alphafold.py](run_alphafold.py#L82-L92)

## Top-Level Schema

Every input JSON is a single object with the following structure:

```json
{
  "name": "My complex",
  "modelSeeds": [1, 2],
  "sequences": [
    {"protein": {...}},
    {"rna": {...}},
    {"dna": {...}},
    {"ligand": {...}}
  ],
  "bondedAtomPairs": [],
  "userCCD": "...",
  "dialect": "alphafold3",
  "version": 4
}
```

The following table defines every top-level field:

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `str` | ✅ | Job name; a sanitized version is used for output filenames |
| `modelSeeds` | `list[int]` | ✅ | Random seeds — one prediction per seed; at least one required |
| `sequences` | `list[Entity]` | ✅ | Ordered list of molecular entities (protein, RNA, DNA, ligand) |
| `bondedAtomPairs` | `list[Bond]` | ❌ | Covalent bonds between atoms (within or across entities) |
| `userCCD` | `str` | ❌ | Inline user-provided CCD (mutually exclusive with `userCCDPath`) |
| `userCCDPath` | `str` | ❌ | Path to user-provided CCD file (mutually exclusive with `userCCD`) |
| `dialect` | `str` | ✅ | Must be `"alphafold3"` |
| `version` | `int` | ✅ | Format version — `1`, `2`, `3`, or `4` |

> [!TIP]
> The `version` field gates feature availability. Use `4` (the latest) to unlock all features including the `description` field on all entity types. Version `2` adds external MSA/template path fields; version `3` adds `userCCDPath`; version `4` adds `description`.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L162-L210), [input.md](docs/input.md#L212-L224)

### Version History

| Version | Feature Added |
|---|---|
| `1` | Initial AlphaFold 3 input format |
| `2` | External MSA and templates via `unpairedMsaPath`, `pairedMsaPath`, `mmcifPath` |
| `3` | External user-provided CCD via `userCCDPath` |
| `4` | Textual `description` field on all entity types |

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L212-L224)

## Sequence Entities

The `sequences` array defines every molecular chain in your complex. Each entry is a dictionary with **exactly one** key — `"protein"`, `"rna"`, `"dna"`, or `"ligand"` — mapping to that entity's specification. Every entity must have a **unique** `id` (an uppercase letter or list of letters). IDs do not need to be alphabetically sorted.

The entity hierarchy and its relationships are illustrated below:

```mermaid
graph TD
    Root["sequences (list)"] --> P["protein"]
    Root --> R["rna"]
    Root --> D["dna"]
    Root --> L["ligand"]

    P --> P_id["id: str | list[str]"]
    P --> P_seq["sequence: str (1-letter AA)"]
    P --> P_mod["modifications (optional)"]
    P --> P_msa["unpairedMsa / pairedMsa (optional)"]
    P --> P_tpl["templates (optional)"]
    P --> P_desc["description (optional, v4+)"]

    R --> R_id["id: str | list[str]"]
    R --> R_seq["sequence: str (A,C,G,U)"]
    R --> R_mod["modifications (optional)"]
    R --> R_msa["unpairedMsa (optional)"]
    R --> R_desc["description (optional, v4+)"]

    D --> D_id["id: str | list[str]"]
    D --> D_seq["sequence: str (A,C,G,T)"]
    D --> D_mod["modifications (optional)"]
    D --> D_desc["description (optional, v4+)"]

    L --> L_id["id: str | list[str]"]
    L --> L_ccd["ccdCodes (optional)"]
    L --> L_smiles["smiles (optional)"]
    L --> L_desc["description (optional, v4+)"]

    L_ccd -.->|mutually exclusive| L_smiles
```

### Homomeric Chains via `id` Lists

When `id` is a list of IDs (e.g. `["A", "B"]`), it creates **multiple copies of the same chain** — a homomeric oligomer. Each ID appears as a separate chain in the output mmCIF.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L230-L280)

## Protein Entity

```json
{
  "protein": {
    "id": "A",
    "sequence": "PVLSCGEWQL",
    "modifications": [
      {"ptmType": "HY3", "ptmPosition": 1},
      {"ptmType": "P1L", "ptmPosition": 5}
    ],
    "description": "Example protein chain",
    "unpairedMsa": "...",
    "unpairedMsaPath": "...",
    "pairedMsa": "...",
    "pairedMsaPath": "...",
    "templates": [...]
  }
}
```

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `str \| list[str]` | Unique chain ID(s); used in output mmCIF and bond references |
| `sequence` | `str` | Amino acid sequence using standard 1-letter codes |
| `modifications` | `list[ProteinMod]` | Optional post-translational modifications (CCD code + 1-based position) |
| `description` | `str` | Optional comment (v4+; not used by the model) |
| `unpairedMsa` | `str` | Inline A3M format MSA (mutually exclusive with `unpairedMsaPath`) |
| `unpairedMsaPath` | `str` | Path to A3M file (mutually exclusive with `unpairedMsa`) |
| `pairedMsa` | `str` | Inline paired A3M MSA (mutually exclusive with `pairedMsaPath`) |
| `pairedMsaPath` | `str` | Path to paired A3M file (mutually exclusive with `pairedMsa`) |
| `templates` | `list[Template]` | Optional structural templates |

**Modification format**: Each entry has `ptmType` (CCD code, e.g. `"TPO"` for phosphothreonine, `"PTR"` for phosphotyrosine) and `ptmPosition` (1-based residue index). The original residue at that position is **replaced** by the modification.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L230-L260), [erk2_phosphorylated.json](examples/erk2_phosphorylated.json#L1-L20)

### Protein MSA Field Combinations

The `unpairedMsa` and `pairedMsa` fields must be **both set or both unset**. The valid combinations are:

| `unpairedMsa` | `pairedMsa` | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| unset / `null` | unset / `null` | Auto-build both MSAs via database search (**recommended default**) |
| non-empty A3M | `""` (empty) | Use provided MSA, run paired-MSA-free (**recommended for custom MSA**) |
| `""` | non-empty A3M | Use paired MSA only, run unpaired-MSA-free (**not recommended**) |
| `""` | `""` | Fully MSA-free (query sequence only) |
| non-empty A3M | non-empty A3M | Use both provided MSAs (expert mode) |

> [!TIP]
> When providing a custom `unpairedMsa`, always set `pairedMsa` to `""` and run with `--resolve_msa_overlaps=false` to prevent deduplication from destroying your carefully crafted MSA positioning.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L452-L530)

## RNA Entity

```json
{
  "rna": {
    "id": "A",
    "sequence": "AGCU",
    "modifications": [
      {"modificationType": "2MG", "basePosition": 1},
      {"modificationType": "5MC", "basePosition": 4}
    ],
    "description": "Modified RNA",
    "unpairedMsa": "...",
    "unpairedMsaPath": "..."
  }
}
```

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `str \| list[str]` | Unique chain ID(s) |
| `sequence` | `str` | RNA sequence using only `A`, `C`, `G`, `U` |
| `modifications` | `list[RnaMod]` | Optional modifications (CCD code + 1-based base position) |
| `description` | `str` | Optional comment (v4+) |
| `unpairedMsa` | `str` | Inline A3M MSA (mutually exclusive with `unpairedMsaPath`) |
| `unpairedMsaPath` | `str` | Path to A3M file (mutually exclusive with `unpairedMsa`) |

**RNA MSA semantics**: Unset/`null` = auto-build; `""` = MSA-free (query only); non-empty = use provided A3M.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L262-L290), [modified_rna.json](examples/modified_rna.json#L1-L21)

## DNA Entity

```json
{
  "dna": {
    "id": "A",
    "sequence": "GACCTCT",
    "modifications": [
      {"modificationType": "6OG", "basePosition": 1},
      {"modificationType": "6MA", "basePosition": 2}
    ],
    "description": "Modified DNA strand"
  }
}
```

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `str \| list[str]` | Unique chain ID(s) |
| `sequence` | `str` | DNA sequence using only `A`, `C`, `G`, `T` |
| `modifications` | `list[DnaMod]` | Optional modifications (CCD code + 1-based base position) |
| `description` | `str` | Optional comment (v4+) |

DNA entities do **not** support custom MSA or templates — AlphaFold 3 handles DNA without external evolutionary information.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L292-L318), [methylated_dna.json](examples/methylated_dna.json#L1-L35)

## Ligand Entity

Ligands are the most flexible entity type, supporting three specification modes:

| Mode | When to Use | Supports Bonds? | Field |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CCD codes** | Standard or user-CCD ligands (e.g. ATP, NAG, MG) | ✅ Yes | `ccdCodes` |
| **SMILES** | Custom ligands not in CCD, no bonds needed | ❌ No | `smiles` |
| **User CCD + codes** | Custom ligands requiring bonds or reference conformers | ✅ Yes | `ccdCodes` + `userCCD`/`userCCDPath` |

```json
{"ligand": {"id": "B", "ccdCodes": ["ATP"], "description": "ATP via CCD code"}},
{"ligand": {"id": "C", "ccdCodes": ["NAG", "NAG", "BMA", "MAN", "MAN"], "description": "Glycan (5 CCD components)"}},
{"ligand": {"id": "D", "smiles": "OC(=O)CCCC[C@@H]1SC[C@@H]2NC(=O)N[C@H]12", "description": "D-Biotin via SMILES"}}
```

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | `str \| list[str]` | Unique chain ID(s); list implies multiple copies |
| `ccdCodes` | `list[str]` | CCD codes (standard or user-defined); mutually exclusive with `smiles` |
| `smiles` | `str` | SMILES string (must be JSON-escaped); mutually exclusive with `ccdCodes` |
| `description` | `str` | Optional comment (v4+) |

**Ions are ligands** — a magnesium ion is simply `{"ligand": {"id": "X", "ccdCodes": ["MG"]}}`.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L320-L390), [calmodulin_4calcium.json](examples/calmodulin_4calcium.json#L1-L23), [streptavidin_biotin_smiles.json](examples/streptavidin_biotin_smiles.json#L1-L23)

### SMILES JSON Escaping

Backslashes in SMILES must be **doubled** in JSON. For example, the SMILES `CCC[C@@H](O)CC\C=C\C=C\C#CC#C\C=C\CO` must be written as:

```json
{"ligand": {"id": "A", "smiles": "CCC[C@@H](O)CC\\C=C\\C=C\\C#CC#C\\C=C\\CO"}}
```

Quick escaping methods:

```bash
# Using jq
jq -R . <<< 'CCC[C@@H](O)CC\C=C\C=C\C#CC#C\C=C\CO'
```

```python
# Using Python
import json
smiles = r'CCC[C@@H](O)CC\C=C\C=C\C#CC#C\C=C\CO'
print(json.dumps(smiles))
```

If RDKit conformer generation fails (indicated by `Failed to construct RDKit reference structure`), either provide a reference structure via [user-provided CCD](#user-provided-ccd) or increase iterations with `--conformer_max_iterations=...`.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L392-L430)

## Covalent Bonds (`bondedAtomPairs`)

The `bondedAtomPairs` field specifies covalent bonds between atoms. Each bond is a pair of atom references, and each atom is addressed by a 3-tuple: **[entity ID, residue index, atom name]**.

```json
"bondedAtomPairs": [
  [["A", 145, "SG"], ["L", 1, "C04"]],
  [["J", 1, "O6"],   ["J", 2, "C1"]]
]
```

| Component | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Entity ID | `str` | The `id` of the entity (e.g. `"A"`, `"B"`) |
| Residue ID | `int` | 1-based index within the chain; for single-residue ligands, always `1` |
| Atom name | `str` | Unique atom name within the residue (lookup in CCD) |

The first example above bonds chain A residue 145 atom SG to chain L residue 1 atom C04 — a typical **covalent ligand** bond. The second bonds two residues within the same entity — typical for **glycan linkages**.

> [!TIP]
> SMILES-defined ligands **cannot** participate in bonds because SMILES provides no atom naming scheme. Use user-provided CCD instead if you need to bond a custom ligand to other entities.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L600-L640), [kras_g12c_sotorasib.json](examples/kras_g12c_sotorasib.json#L1-L26), [rnaseb_glycosylated.json](examples/rnaseb_glycosylated.json#L1-L30)

### Defining Glycans

Glycans are multi-component ligands bound to a protein. The pattern is: define a single ligand entity with all CCD components, then specify the bond from protein to the first glycan component plus all intra-glycan bonds.

For a glycan with 4 components (CMP1–CMP4) branching off an asparagine:

```
 ⋮
ALA            CMP4
 |              |
ASN ―― CMP1 ―― CMP2
 |              |
ALA            CMP3
 ⋮
```

You need: (1) protein chain A, (2) ligand chain B with `["CMP1","CMP2","CMP3","CMP4"]`, and (3) bonds for ASN→CMP1, CMP1→CMP2, CMP2→CMP3, CMP2→CMP4.

A real example — the **Man₃GlcNAc₂** N-linked core glycan on RNase B:

```json
"sequences": [
  {"protein": {"id": "A", "sequence": "KETAAAKFERQ..."}},
  {"ligand": {"id": "B", "ccdCodes": ["NAG","NAG","BMA","MAN","MAN"]}}
],
"bondedAtomPairs": [
  [["A", 34, "ND2"], ["B", 1, "C1"]],
  [["B", 1, "O4"],   ["B", 2, "C1"]],
  [["B", 2, "O4"],   ["B", 3, "C1"]],
  [["B", 3, "O3"],   ["B", 4, "C1"]],
  [["B", 3, "O6"],   ["B", 5, "C1"]]
]
```

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L641-L670), [rnaseb_glycosylated.json](examples/rnaseb_glycosylated.json#L1-L30)

## Structural Templates

Templates are supported **only for protein chains**. Each template maps query residues to residues in a structural template mmCIF:

```json
"templates": [
  {
    "mmcif": "...",
    "mmcifPath": "template.cif",
    "queryIndices": [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6],
    "templateIndices": [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 8]
  }
]
```

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `mmcif` | `str` | Inline mmCIF string (mutually exclusive with `mmcifPath`) |
| `mmcifPath` | `str` | Path to mmCIF file (mutually exclusive with `mmcif`) |
| `queryIndices` | `list[int]` | 0-based indices in the query sequence |
| `templateIndices` | `list[int]` | 0-based indices in the template (accounting for unresolved residues) |

**Critical**: `templateIndices` must account for **unresolved residues** in the mmCIF. If the template has unresolved residues 1–3 followed by resolved residues 4–7, aligning query residues to 4–7 requires template indices `3, 4, 5, 6` (0-based). The mmCIF must contain exactly **one chain** — multi-chain mmCIFs will raise an error.

### Template-Free and MSA-Only Modes

| Goal | Configuration |
|---|---|
| Template-free (still auto-build MSA) | `"templates": []` |
| Template-free + custom MSA | `"unpairedMsa": "...", "pairedMsa": "", "templates": []` |
| Custom MSA, let AF3 search templates | `"unpairedMsa": "...", "pairedMsa": ""` (omit `templates` or set to `null`) |

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L535-L598)

## MSA Pairing Strategy

MSA pairing matters only for **multimers** — it determines how sequences from different chains are aligned into the same MSA row. Naive concatenation can place sequences from different organisms in the same row, producing incorrect evolutionary coupling signals.

AlphaFold 3 internally pairs sequences by matching **UniProt organism IDs** in the `pairedMsa`. However, the **recommended approach** for custom MSAs is:

1. Manually pair sequences (or use pairing software) and provide them via `unpairedMsa` only.
2. Set `pairedMsa` to `""`.
3. Run with `--resolve_msa_overlaps=false`.

This gives you exact control over sequence placement, rather than relying on name-matching heuristics. For example, to pair chains `DEEP` and `MIND` on organisms A and C:

```
> query          > query
DEEP             MIND
> match 1 (org A)  > match 1 (org A)
D--P             M--D
> match 2 (org B)  ----          ← padding for unpaired row
DD-P             ----
> match 3 (org C)  > match 2 (org C)
DD-P             MIN-
```

The concatenated result preserves organism-level pairing:

```
> query
DEEPMIND
> match 1 + match 1      ← organism A (paired)
D--PM--D
> match 2 + padding      ← organism B (unpaired)
DD-P----
> match 3 + match 2      ← organism C (paired)
DD-PMIN-
```

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L530-L590)

## User-Providved CCD

When SMILES is insufficient (you need bonds, custom atom names, or reference coordinates), define custom molecules in [CCD mmCIF format](https://www.wwpdb.org/data/ccd#mmcifFormat):

| Delivery Method | Field | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Inline string | `userCCD` | Newlines must be `\n`; single quotes around values |
| External file | `userCCDPath` | Plain text, gzip, xz, or zstd compressed |

Assign a **non-clashing name** (e.g. `"LIG-1"`) — avoid underscores. The custom component is then referenced via `ccdCodes` in a ligand entity or `ptmType`/`modificationType` in polymer modifications.

### User CCD for Polymer Modifications

Custom components can also replace residues in polymer chains:

```json
{
  "protein": {
    "id": "A",
    "sequence": "MDQHQAFKEATELLEKMKTSSDEERVEYLRKAVRLFNLTSEGQQGELVGKFKEAGVLIRAVDLS",
    "modifications": [{"ptmType": "MYMOD", "ptmPosition": 30}]
  }
}
```

The user CCD entry for `MYMOD` should describe a **peptide-linking** component with the correct backbone atoms and bond graph for its position (mid-chain vs. terminal).

### Mandatory CCD mmCIF Fields

**Singular fields** (single value per component):

| Field | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `_chem_comp.id` | ✅ | Must match `_data` record; no `_` or `#` characters |
| `_chem_comp.name` | ❌ | Full name or `?` |
| `_chem_comp.type` | ✅ | Typically `non-polymer` |
| `_chem_comp.formula` | ❌ | Chemical formula or `?` |
| `_chem_comp.mon_nstd_parent_comp_id` | ❌ | Parent ID or `?` |
| `_chem_comp.pdbx_synonyms` | ❌ | Synonyms or `?` |
| `_chem_comp.formula_weight` | ❌ | Molecular weight or `?` |

**Per-atom fields** (`_chem_comp_atom` loop):

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `comp_id`, `atom_id`, `type_symbol`, `charge` | Atom identity and element |
| `pdbx_leaving_atom_flag` | Leaving atom flag (default `N`) |
| `pdbx_model_Cartn_{x,y,z}_ideal` | Ideal coordinates (fallback if RDKit conformer fails) |

**Per-bond fields** (`_chem_comp_bond` loop):

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `atom_id_1`, `atom_id_2` | Bonded atom pair |
| `value_order` | Bond order (`SING`, `DOUB`, `TRIP`, etc.) |
| `pdbx_aromatic_flag` | Aromatic flag (`Y`/`N`) |

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L730-L870)

### Conformer Generation Fallback Chain

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[RDKit conformer] -->|success| B[Use RDKit coordinates]
    A -->|failure| C[Ideal coordinates in CCD?]
    C -->|yes| D[Use ideal coordinates]
    C -->|no| E[Reference coordinates + pre-cutoff date?]
    E -->|yes| F[Use reference coordinates]
    E -->|no| G[All zeros → NaN confidence output]
```

If conformer generation fails, try increasing `--conformer_max_iterations=...` before resorting to ideal coordinates.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L680-L710)

## AlphaFold Server JSON Compatibility

The [AlphaFold Server](https://alphafoldserver.com/) uses a different JSON format (top-level is a **list**, not an object). `run_alphafold.py` auto-detects the dialect and converts `alphafoldserver` → `alphafold3`.

| Aspect | `alphafold3` | `alphafoldserver` |
|---|---|---|
| Top-level | Single object | List of objects |
| Seeds | Required explicitly | `"modelSeeds": []` → random seed |
| Glycans | Full support | **Converter raises error** |
| Ions | `ligand` with `ccdCodes: ["MG"]` | Separate `ion` entity type |
| Entity IDs | User-specified `id` field | Auto-assigned (A, B, …, Z, AA, BA, …) |
| Covalent bonds | `bondedAtomPairs` | Not supported |

**Important**: If you pass an `alphafoldserver`-style JSON **without** a top-level list, `run_alphafold.py` will raise an error — the list wrapper is the detection signal.

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L40-L100)

## Complete Reference Example

This annotated example shows every feature in a single JSON (sequences are abbreviated for clarity):

```json
{
  "name": "Hello fold",
  "modelSeeds": [10, 42],
  "sequences": [
    {
      "protein": {
        "id": "A",
        "sequence": "PVLSCGEWQL",
        "modifications": [
          {"ptmType": "HY3", "ptmPosition": 1},
          {"ptmType": "P1L", "ptmPosition": 5}
        ],
        "description": "Protein with PTMs and custom MSA",
        "unpairedMsa": ">query\nPVLSCGEWQL\n>hit\nPVLS-GEWQL",
        "pairedMsa": ""
      }
    },
    {
      "protein": {
        "id": "B",
        "sequence": "RPACQLW",
        "templates": [{
          "mmcifPath": "template_b.cif",
          "queryIndices": [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6],
          "templateIndices": [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 8]
        }]
      }
    },
    {
      "dna": {
        "id": "C",
        "sequence": "GACCTCT",
        "modifications": [{"modificationType": "6OG", "basePosition": 1}]
      }
    },
    {
      "rna": {
        "id": "E",
        "sequence": "AGCU",
        "modifications": [{"modificationType": "2MG", "basePosition": 1}],
        "unpairedMsa": ">query\nAGCU"
      }
    },
    {
      "ligand": {"id": ["F","G","H"], "ccdCodes": ["ATP"]}
    },
    {
      "ligand": {"id": "I", "ccdCodes": ["NAG", "FUC"]}
    },
    {
      "ligand": {"id": "Z", "smiles": "CC(=O)OC1C[NH+]2CCC1CC2"}
    }
  ],
  "bondedAtomPairs": [
    [["A", 1, "CA"], ["G", 1, "CHA"]],
    [["I", 1, "O6"], ["I", 2, "C1"]]
  ],
  "dialect": "alphafold3",
  "version": 4
}
```

Sources: [input.md](docs/input.md#L960-L1056)

## Real-World Example Gallery

The `examples/` directory contains 12 ready-to-run input JSONs covering the major use cases:

| Example File | Complex Type | Key Features |
|---|---|---|
| `ubiquitin_monomer.json` | Single protein | Minimal input — just sequence + seed |
| `barnase_barstar.json` | Protein–protein dimer | Two protein chains, no modifications |
| `tetr_homodimer.json` | Homodimer | `id: ["A","B"]` for symmetric dimer |
| `erk2_phosphorylated.json` | Phosphorylated protein | `modifications` with TPO/PTR |
| `calmodulin_4calcium.json` | Protein + ions | 4 Ca²⁺ ligands via `id: ["B","C","D","E"]` |
| `u1a_rna_hairpin.json` | Protein–RNA complex | Protein chain + RNA chain |
| `modified_rna.json` | Modified RNA | PSU, 5MC, OMG modifications |
| `methylated_dna.json` | Methylated dsDNA | Two DNA strands with 5CM at CpG sites |
| `tetr_dimer_dna.json` | Protein–DNA complex | Homodimer + two DNA strands |
| `tetr_dimer_tetracycline.json` | Protein + drug | Homodimer + 2 tetracycline (TAC) ligands |
| `kras_g12c_sotorasib.json` | Covalent inhibitor | `bondedAtomPairs` linking protein SG to ligand C25 |
| `rnaseb_glycosylated.json` | Glycosylated protein | N-linked glycan with 5 `bondedAtomPairs` |
| `streptavidin_biotin_smiles.json` | SMILES ligand | Biotin defined via SMILES string |

Sources: [ubiquitin_monomer.json](examples/ubiquitin_monomer.json#L1-L16), [barnase_barstar.json](examples/barnase_barstar.json#L1-L23), [tetr_homodimer.json](examples/tetr_homodimer.json#L1-L16), [erk2_phosphorylated.json](examples/erk2_phosphorylated.json#L1-L20), [calmodulin_4calcium.json](examples/calmodulin_4calcium.json#L1-L23), [u1a_rna_hairpin.json](examples/u1a_rna_hairpin.json#L1-L23), [modified_rna.json](examples/modified_rna.json#L1-L21), [methylated_dna.json](examples/methylated_dna.json#L1-L35), [tetr_dimer_dna.json](examples/tetr_dimer_dna.json#L1-L30), [tetr_dimer_tetracycline.json](examples/tetr_dimer_tetracycline.json#L1-L23), [kras_g12c_sotorasib.json](examples/kras_g12c_sotorasib.json#L1-L26), [rnaseb_glycosylated.json](examples/rnaseb_glycosylated.json#L1-L30), [streptavidin_biotin_smiles.json](examples/streptavidin_biotin_smiles.json#L1-L23)

---

**Next steps**: Once your input JSON is ready, proceed to [Quick Start](2-quick-start) to run your first prediction, or explore [Input Examples and Patterns](22-input-examples-and-patterns) for more advanced composition patterns. For understanding what the model produces, see [Output Format and Metrics](15-output-format-and-metrics).

# Latest Updates



AlphaFold 3 is iterating fast. Since the landmark [v3.0.4 release](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/releases) in late July 2026, a steady stream of patches has landed — driven largely by one engineer, [Augustin Zidek](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/c0f97eda2f1f482fd94d3a38bece18c7069b4a5c), and a surprising number of community PRs and issue reports. Here's what changed, what matters, and what's still rough around the edges.

## v3.0.4: The "Runs Everywhere" Release

The official [v3.0.4 changelog](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/releases/tag/v3.0.4) frames the release around two headline features: **CPU-only execution** and **Apple Silicon GPU support**. The practical impact is real but nuanced.

### Apple Silicon Arrives

The [commit adding Apple Silicon GPU support](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/85c4d20505fd5cef05eac22b534d4e793971ae69) was heavily inspired by [PR #699](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/699) from @SuhasSrinivasan, and the release notes claim **roughly 3x faster inference than CPU on a MacBook Pro M3**. That's a meaningful speedup for a laptop, but it's worth keeping perspective: a data-center H100 still obliterates it. The real win is accessibility — researchers who don't have queue access to an A100 can now iterate on inputs and validate pipelines locally.

The JAX backend was refactored to make this possible. The old `--use_cpu_only` flag was [replaced with `--jax_backend`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/98a15dcf0cf09f8e5e2b08410b0c4e8be5308e05), which is explicitly designed for "future expandability." This is the right structural call — a boolean flag for CPU-only was already a leaky abstraction once Metal entered the picture. Expect `--jax_backend` to grow more accepted values as JAX's backend landscape evolves.

### CPU-Only: Useful, Not Fast

CPU-only mode works. It's documented as slow. If you're running anything beyond a tiny peptide on CPU, "slow" undersells it — think hours where a GPU takes minutes. The value proposition is CI/CD validation, input testing, and environments where no GPU exists at all. For actual research workloads, this is a last resort.

### JAX and Haiku Bumps

v3.0.4 updated **JAX from 0.9.1 to 0.10.2** and **Tokamax from 0.0.11 to 0.0.12**. Per the release notes, this should "significantly speed up inference times and fix unified memory support on Blackwell GPUs." However, post-release, a [Haiku dependency was bumped from 0.0.16 to 0.0.17](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/e82e974eebffd0408a409f1cb61a0fbca56e4046), specifically addressing [Issue #715](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/715). Dependency versioning in the JAX ecosystem remains fragile — a minor Haiku bump was enough to break things for users on the previous version. If you're running custom environments outside Docker, pin your versions.

### Other v3.0.4 Highlights

| Area | Change | Credit |
|---|---|---|
| Performance | Reduced memory for outer product mean (2 einsums → 1) | @mooreneural |
| Output | Chain IDs added to summary confidence JSON | @ntnn19 |
| Validation | Early RNG seed validation as uint32 | @ntnn19 |
| Storage | Google Cloud Storage (`gs://`) path support via `etils.epath` | — |
| Docs | User-provided CCD for custom modified residues | @Fred-Jing |

## Post-v3.0.4 Commits: Robustness and Performance

Since the v3.0.4 tag, the repository has seen continued patching — almost entirely from Augustin Zidek, often incorporating or adapting community contributions. The activity cluster from August 11–19, 2026 is particularly dense.

```mermaid
timeline
    title AlphaFold 3 Post-v3.0.4 Development Timeline
    section July 2026
        Jul 23 : --jax_backend replaces --use_cpu_only
        Jul 28 : Apple Silicon GPU support lands
        Jul 29 : Omit license from output mmCIF when save_terms_of_use=false
    section August 2026
        Aug 11 : Compilation buckets (128, 384) for small proteins
        Aug 11 : Fix empty template maps from AF < 3.0.4
        Aug 12 : Haiku 0.0.16 → 0.0.17 bump
        Aug 12 : Fix resource leak in sharded Jackhmmer/Nhmmer
        Aug 12 : Better binary check error messages
        Aug 12 : Expose Hmmsearch CPU count as flag
        Aug 13 : Make data tests robust to RDKit/CCD updates
        Aug 14 : Version string → v3.0.4
        Aug 14 : Fix RNA sequence in fill_missing_fields
        Aug 14 : Include unit tests for folding input
        Aug 19 : Validate templates is a list
```

### Small Protein Compilation Buckets

[This commit](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/29596b97021cfc941b1993249969c4f268efdbab) adds compilation buckets of size 128 and 384, inspired by [PR #706](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/706) from @teerthsharma. AlphaFold 3 compiles XLA kernels per bucket size, and previously the smallest bucket was too large for short peptides — meaning a 50-residue protein paid the compilation cost of a much larger one. This is a real quality-of-life improvement for anyone doing large-scale screening of small proteins or peptides.

### Resource Leak Fix

The [fix for leaked resources in sharded Jackhmmer/Nhmmer](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/039eb598b4bbe773b0d434769a963b777a5522cc) was inspired by [PR #705](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/705). When a sharded subprocess errored out, resources weren't being cleaned up. In HPC environments running hundreds of folds in sequence, leaked file descriptors and subprocess handles eventually bite you. This is the kind of bug that's invisible in single-run testing but catastrophic in batch pipelines.

### Hmmsearch CPU Control

Two commits — [exposing the Hmmsearch CPU count](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/c1ca92891b2904a69b1605fbe92d812edd5da390) and [exposing it as a flag](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/e2de24b52bd6b71afee062ddd1189dad9717043c) — give users explicit control over Hmmsearch parallelism. On shared SLURM nodes where you've requested `--cpus-per-task=32`, you probably don't want Hmmsearch silently consuming all of them. This is a small but important operational control.

### Template and Input Validation Fixes

Several commits target input robustness:

- **[Templates validated as a list](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/c0f97eda2f1f482fd94d3a38bece18c7069b4a5c)** — directly addresses the crash reported in [Issue #720](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/720), where passing a string instead of a dict for a template caused an `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'keys'`.
- **[Empty template maps from AF < 3.0.4](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/25461454b174c2a21f509554c086bd3c26e8e06a)** — inspired by [PR #710](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/710), handles backward compatibility when loading template maps written by earlier versions.
- **[RNA sequence fix in fill_missing_fields](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/97d20234c6eb89e8d05376e9eecc9321e60a559b)** — adapted from [PR #704](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/704), ensures the original (unmodified) RNA sequence is used.

### Better Error Messages

The [binary check improvement](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/501f7a9056f1ce20580c45ce588a9a4a4a01dc1b) makes `shutil.which` failures more informative. When a required binary (like `jackhmmer` or `hmmsearch`) isn't found on PATH, the error now tells you what's missing instead of failing with a cryptic traceback. Small change, outsized impact on first-time users.

## Active Issues Worth Watching

The open issue tracker reveals where the project's growing pains are concentrated: **GPU compatibility**, **performance regressions**, and **model correctness questions**.

### Autotuning Cache Miss and Inference Slowdown (Issue #742)

[Issue #742](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/742) reports that after updating to the latest code, running on an RTX A6000 triggers an `Autotuning cache miss for PallasTritonGatedLinearUnit` warning, and **GPU inference time increased by at least 80 seconds** for an 898-residue protein compared to v3.0.1. This is a concrete performance regression that likely stems from the JAX/Tokamax update path. If Pallas Triton kernels can't find their autotuning cache, they fall back to slower compilation or execution paths. Anyone on non-H100 GPUs should benchmark before upgrading.

### Segmentation Fault on RTX PRO 6000 (Issue #735)

[Issue #735](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/735) documents a segfault in `jax._src.compiler.backend_compile_and_load` on an RTX PRO 6000. The traceback is entirely within JAX/XLA compilation — AlphaFold 3's code never gets control. This is almost certainly a JAX/GPU driver compatibility issue, not an AlphaFold bug per se, but it illustrates how the JAX ecosystem's hardware support matrix remains a source of pain for anyone not on the blessed A100/H100 configuration.

### Potential Model Correctness Issue: ref_space_uid Layout (Issue #730)

[Issue #730](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/730) raises a more serious concern: in `atom_cross_attention.py`, `ref_space_uid` is in token layout but is being converted using `queries_to_keys`, which may produce incorrect `offsets_valid` masks. The reporter found that for a 1171-atom input, only 45 rows in `offsets_valid` contained nonzero values. If confirmed, this is a **model correctness bug**, not just a performance issue — it would mean the atom cross-attention is masking out positions it shouldn't. The issue is open and awaiting confirmation from the maintainers.

### Feature Proposal: Preflight Validation (Issue #732)

[Issue #732](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/732) proposes a `--validate_input_only` flag that would parse and validate input JSON without launching the data pipeline or inference. The motivation is solid: on shared clusters, you don't want to discover an input error after your job has waited 4 hours in the queue and then burned 30 minutes of H100 time on the data pipeline. The proposal is deliberately narrow — reuse existing validation, add a single CLI flag, no new schema. This fits the project's stated preference for small, incremental changes.

## The Bigger Picture

The trajectory of AlphaFold 3 post-v3.0.4 is clear: **democratize access and harden the operational experience**. The Apple Silicon and CPU-only support lower the hardware barrier. The compilation buckets, Hmmsearch CPU flags, and resource leak fixes address the operational realities of running at scale. The input validation improvements (and proposals) target the most common class of user error.

But the GPU compatibility issues (#735, #742) are a reminder that AlphaFold 3's relationship with JAX and XLA is a double-edged sword. JAX provides hardware portability in theory; in practice, the autotuning caches, compilation paths, and driver compat requirements mean that **"runs on NVIDIA" is not a monolithic guarantee** — it runs reliably on A100/H100, less so on consumer and professional GPUs. And the potential correctness issue in #730, if confirmed, would be the most significant finding since release, since it touches the core model's attention mechanism.

The community contribution pattern is also notable. Many of the post-release fixes are "inspired by" external PRs (#704, #705, #706, #710) rather than direct merges. This suggests the internal Google Piper workflow re-implements community suggestions rather than merging them directly — standard for Google-scale repos, but it means contributor credit flows through commit messages rather than the GitHub PR graph.

| Version | Key Theme | Hardware Impact |
|---|---|---|
| v3.0.0 | Initial release | NVIDIA A100/H100 only |
| v3.0.1 | Operational flags, template control | Same |
| v3.0.2 | Sharded MSA, Blackwell support, Tokamax | NVIDIA Blackwell added |
| v3.0.3 | Apache 2.0 license, Python 3.14 | Same |
| **v3.0.4** | **CPU-only, Apple Silicon, JAX 0.10.2** | **x86 CPU, Apple M-series GPU** |
| Post-v3.0.4 | Robustness patches, small-protein perf | Stabilization |

If you're upgrading, the practical advice is straightforward: **pin to v3.0.4, benchmark your GPU**, and watch [Issue #730](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/730) and [Issue #742](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/742) for resolution. The codebase is moving fast, but the edges are still sharp.

# Issues and Feedbacks



The AlphaFold 3 open-source repository has accumulated a revealing set of issues since its release. They paint a picture of a system that delivers remarkable structural predictions but operates under significant hardware constraints, has rough edges in its chemistry support, and leaves its most demanding users -- those pushing beyond the standard single-protein-on-H100 workflow -- to navigate undocumented territory. Below is a structured analysis of the recurring pain points, with direct links to the original issues and relevant commits.

## The Pain Map at a Glance

| Category | Key Issue | Severity | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| GPU Performance | Runtime 2x reported on H100 | High | Open |
| GPU Compatibility | Segfault on RTX PRO 6000 | High | Open |
| GPU Performance | Autotuning cache miss, +80s on A6000 | Medium | Open |
| Memory / OOM | Rematerialization failure at 5000+ tokens | High | Open |
| Memory / OOM | `pair_transition_shard_spec` undocumented for non-40/80 GB | Medium | Closed |
| Model Correctness | `ref_space_uid` layout bug in atom cross-attention | High | Open |
| Model Correctness | Documentation mismatch: MSA used for template search | Low | Closed |
| Input / Pipeline | Preflight validation mode requested | Medium | Open |
| Input / Pipeline | Internal I/O error during template parsing | Medium | Open |
| Input / Pipeline | Template JSON parsing `AttributeError` | Medium | Closed |
| Chemistry | Bond order lost in output mmCIF | Medium | Open |
| Chemistry | Polymer-polymer covalent bonds unsupported | Medium | Open |
| Chemistry | O-glycan glycosidic torsion unconstrained | Medium | Closed |
| Chemistry | PTM and terminal capping ambiguity | Low | Closed |
| Perf Optimization | Redundant featurization across seeds | Medium | Open |
| Perf Optimization | Custom database/template appending fails | Medium | Closed |

---

## GPU Performance: The Gap Between Reported and Actual Runtime

This is arguably the most impactful open issue cluster. Users consistently report that real-world inference times substantially exceed the numbers in the [performance documentation](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/blob/main/docs/performance.md).

### Runtime 2x Higher Than Documented

[Issue #609](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/609) reports that on an H100 with pools of 20-35 proteins near the 5000-token limit, inference takes **~45 minutes** -- roughly **twice** the documented runtime for that token count. The user is using a properly configured SLURM environment with `--cpus-per-task=32` and 193 GB mem-per-gpu. The issue has been open since January 2026 and last updated September 2026, suggesting this is a persistent, unresolved discrepancy.

This matters because the performance doc is the primary reference users consult for capacity planning. If those numbers are only achievable under idealized (single-input, warm cache?) conditions, the documentation should say so explicitly.

### Autotuning Cache Miss and Regression from v3.0.1

[Issue #742](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/742) identifies a **regression**: after updating to the latest version, an RTX A6000 produces `Autotuning cache miss for PallasTritonGatedLinearUnit` warnings, and **inference for a single seed on an 898-residue protein is at least 80 seconds slower** compared to v3.0.1. This suggests a JAX/Pallas Triton kernel autotuning change introduced a performance regression for non-H100/A100 GPUs. The fact that autotuning cache misses occur means the Pallas Triton kernels are falling back to slower paths or recompiling on every run.

### Segmentation Fault on RTX PRO 6000

[Issue #735](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/735) reports a hard segfault in `jax._src.compiler.backend_compile_and_load` on an RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell, 96 GB VRAM). The traceback terminates in XLA's compilation path, which points to a JAX/XLA compatibility issue rather than an AlphaFold 3 logic bug. This is notable because the [official system requirements](https://google-deepmind-alphafold3.mintlify.app) specify Compute Capability 8.0+ (Ampere), and Blackwell (CC 9.0+) should theoretically be supported -- but the segfault suggests otherwise.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[User runs AF3 on non-H100 GPU] --> B{GPU Architecture?}
    B -->|Ampere A100/A40| C[Works, but slower than reported]
    B -->|Ada RTX A6000/6000| D[Autotuning cache miss<br/>+80s regression]
    B -->|Blackwell RTX PRO 6000| E[Segmentation fault<br/>in XLA compile]
    B -->|Hopper H100| F[Works as documented<br/>if single input]
    C --> G[Issue #609: 2x runtime gap]
    D --> H[Issue #742: Pallas Triton fallback]
    E --> I[Issue #735: JAX/XLA crash]
```

**Takeaway:** AlphaFold 3 is effectively a first-class citizen only on H100/A100. Users on consumer or workstation GPUs face a spectrum from "slower than advertised" to "hard crash." The [Apple Silicon GPU support](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/85c4d20505fd5cef05eac22b534d4e793971ae69) added in v3.0.4 (roughly 3x faster than CPU on M3) shows the team is willing to broaden hardware support, but NVIDIA workstation GPUs remain poorly validated.

---

## Memory and OOM: The Frontier of Large Systems

### Rematerialization Failure

[Issue #432](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/432) captures the experience of running systems with **>5000 residues** using unified memory. The XLA rematerialization pass emits:

```
Can't reduce memory use below -20.61GiB by rematerialization;
only reduced to 28.35GiB, down from 28.35GiB originally
```

The user is on an H100 with `TF_FORCE_UNIFIED_MEMORY=true` and `XLA_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=3.2`. The negative target (`-20.61GiB`) suggests XLA's cost model has fundamentally miscalculated the memory budget. This issue has been open since May 2025 with only limited guidance from maintainers.

### Undocumented `pair_transition_shard_spec` for Non-Standard VRAM

[Issue #717](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/717) (closed) raises a practical concern: the performance doc only provides `pair_transition_shard_spec` recommendations for 40 GB and 80 GB VRAM. Users with 32 GB, 48 GB, or 96 GB GPUs are left to guess. The user's intuition -- first find the max token count without sharding, then choose a sharding spec -- is reasonable but undocumented. The issue was closed without a concrete recommendation, which is itself informative: the team likely hasn't benchmarked these configurations.

### The `RuntimeWarning: overflow` Canary

[Issue #236](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/236) reports `RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in reduce` during featurization of large inputs (5878 tokens) on an A40 with unified memory. The user notes that outputs appear reasonable despite the warning. This issue has been open since December 2024 -- making it one of the oldest open issues -- suggesting the overflow is a known but low-priority edge case in NumPy reduction operations during featurization.

---

## Model Correctness: A Layout Bug and a Documentation Mismatch

### `ref_space_uid` Layout Conversion Bug

[Issue #730](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/730) identifies what appears to be a **real correctness bug** in [`atom_cross_attention.py`](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/blob/main/src/alphafold3/model/network/atom_cross_attention.py). The code converts `batch.ref_structure.ref_space_uid` using `queries_to_keys` layout conversion, but `ref_space_uid` is in token layout. This causes `offsets_valid` to mask out almost all positions -- in a test with 1171 atoms, only 45 rows contained nonzero values. The reporter suggests the fix is to use `queries_ref_space_uid` as the source tensor instead.

This is significant because the atom cross-attention module is central to AlphaFold 3's structure prediction. If `offsets_valid` is incorrectly masking valid positions, the model is effectively ignoring most reference structure information during cross-attention. Whether this meaningfully impacts prediction quality is unclear, but the bug warrants investigation.

### MSA-Template Documentation Mismatch (Resolved)

[Issue #729](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/729) (closed) correctly identified that the documentation states only UniRef90 MSA is used for the template search HMM profile, while the implementation actually uses the **merged UniRef90 + small BFD + MGnify** unpaired MSA. This was a documentation-only issue, but it highlights a pattern: the pipeline's actual behavior diverges from what the docstrings describe, which matters for users who need to reason about what information their templates are derived from.

---

## Input Pipeline: Robustness and Usability Gaps

### Preflight Validation Mode Request

[Issue #732](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/732) proposes adding `--validate_input_only` to `run_alphafold.py` -- a flag that validates input JSON and exits before allocating GPU time or launching the data pipeline. The motivation is solid: for complex inputs with custom CCD components, user-provided MSAs, bonded atom pairs, and modifications, input errors currently surface only after expensive computation has begun. The proposal is deliberately narrow (reuse existing validation, add a CLI entry point) and consistent with the repository's preference for small changes.

This is a quality-of-life improvement that would particularly benefit batch processing on shared HPC clusters where GPU-hours are scarce and job scheduling overhead is high. As of this writing, the maintainers have not responded.

### Internal I/O Error During Template Parsing

[Issue #714](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/714) demonstrates a fragile failure mode: AlphaFold 3 processes several inputs successfully, then crashes on a specific input with `OSError: [Errno 5] Input/output error` while reading an mmCIF template file. The error originates in `structure_stores.py` calling `filepath.read_text()`. This could be a filesystem issue (NFS, Lustre, or scratch disk corruption) or a race condition in template file access. The user notes the same input *always* fails on retry, which rules out transient I/O errors and suggests either a corrupted template file or a systematic path resolution bug for certain PDB IDs.

### Template JSON Parsing Error (Resolved)

[Issue #720](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/720) (closed) exposed an `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'keys'` when parsing template data in `folding_input.py`. The user had formatted templates as strings rather than dicts. This was addressed by [commit c0f97ed](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/c0f97eda2f1f482fd94d3a38bece18c7069b4a5c), which added validation that templates must be a list. The fix is good, but the original error message was unhelpful -- a case where the preflight validation proposed in #732 would have caught the problem immediately.

---

## Chemistry Limitations: Where AlphaFold 3's Reach Exceeds Its Grasp

### Bond Order Lost in Output

[Issue #189](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/189), open since December 2024, reports that output mmCIF files omit `_chem_comp_bond.*` fields, so double bonds specified in the input (e.g., C5B=C7B in CCD residue AC1) are **lost**. In visualization tools like PyMOL and Chimera, the double bond disappears. The user asks whether this undermines inference accuracy -- a fair question, since incorrect bond order information could affect the diffusion module's atom position refinement. This remains unanswered.

### Polymer-Polymer Covalent Bonds Unsupported

[Issue #152](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/152) documents that covalent bonds between polymer entities (protein-DNA, protein-RNA) are explicitly **not supported**. The code silently reduces such bonds:

```
Reducing number of bonds for top1_dna_topotecan_hg from 1 to 0,
of which 1 are polymer-polymer bonds and 0 are bad bonds.
```

The user's workaround -- treating a single DNA residue as a ligand -- is creative but unvalidated. This is a hard limitation of the current architecture, not a bug, but it significantly constrains AlphaFold 3's applicability to covalent drug-target complexes.

### O-Glycan Glycosidic Torsion Geometry

[Issue #701](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/701) (closed) provides a detailed quantitative analysis: when modeling O-linked GalNAc glycosylation via `bondedAtomPairs`, the glycosidic phi dihedral (O5-C1-OG-CB) is **unconstrained** across seeds, with standard deviations of 36-110 degrees per site. The expected range for alpha-O-GalNAc is -40 to -80 degrees (exo-anomeric effect). Zero out of 14 sites had >=80% of models in the correct alpha range. The user is working around this with post-hoc GlycoShape refinement.

This isn't a bug per se -- AlphaFold 3's diffusion module has no explicit torsion potentials for glycosidic linkages -- but it's a significant limitation for the glycobiology community that the output gives no warning about.

### PTM and Terminal Capping Ambiguity

[Issue #716](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/716) (closed) raises three practical questions about using PTMs and terminal caps: (1) should the MSA step use the unmodified residue? (2) can AF3 ignore a residue's identity during MSA/template search? (3) how to model terminal capping groups like acetyl (ACE) that lack CA/CB atoms? These are workflow-level questions that the documentation doesn't address, leaving users to discover the answers experimentally.

---

## Performance Optimization Opportunities

### Redundant Featurization Across Seeds

[Issue #675](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/675) points out a clear inefficiency: when running inference with multiple seeds, `featurisation.featurise_input` calls `data_pipeline.process_item` repeatedly on the same inputs. Within `WholePdbPipeline.process_structure`, the random seed is only used once at the end (in `RefStructure.compute_features`). The user proposes factoring out the seed-independent computation from the loop, which could significantly reduce data pipeline overhead for multi-seed runs. The user offered to draft a PR but received no response as of this writing.

### Small-Protein Compilation Buckets

[Commit 29596b9](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/29596b97021cfc941b1993249969c4f268efdbab) added compilation buckets of size 128 and 384 to make running small proteins faster by default. This was inspired by [PR #706](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/706) from community contributor @teerthsharma. This is a meaningful optimization because JAX's JIT compilation cost is amortized over the bucket, and small proteins were previously bucketed into sizes designed6144, paying a disproportionate compilation overhead.

### Custom Database Extension Fails

[Issue #737](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/737) (closed) reports that appending custom CIF files to the template directory and their sequences to `pdb_seqres_2022_09_28.fasta` does not work. This is a common use case for users who want to fold against templates not in the static 2022-09-28 PDB snapshot. The issue was closed but the resolution is unclear -- if the approach is simply unsupported, the documentation should state this explicitly rather than letting users discover it through errors.

---

## What the Issue Patterns Reveal

```mermaid
timeline
    title AlphaFold 3 Issue Timeline by Theme
    section 2024 Q4
        Chemistry : #189 Bond order lost (Dec)
        Chemistry : #152 Polymer bonds unsupported (Dec)
        Perf : #236 Overflow warning (Dec)
    section 2025 Q1-Q2
        Memory : #432 Rematerialization failure (May)
    section 2025 Q4
        Perf : #609 2x runtime gap (Jan 2026)
    section 2026 Q1
        %% Placeholder to maintain chronological order
    section 2026 Q2
        Perf : #675 Redundant featurization (May)
        Chemistry : #189,#152 Still open
    section 2026 Q3
        Model : #730 ref_space_uid layout bug (Aug)
        Docs : "#729 MSA-template mismatch (Aug, closed)"
        Input : #732 Preflight validation request (Aug)
        Input : #714 I/O error (Aug)
        Perf : #717 shard_spec for 48/96 GB (Aug, closed)
        Chemistry : #716 PTM/capping questions (Aug, closed)
        Chemistry : #701 O-glycan torsion (Jul, closed)
    section 2026 Q3-Q4
        GPU : #735 Segfault RTX PRO 6000 (Sep)
        GPU : #742 Autotuning cache miss (Sep)
        Input : #737 Custom DB append fails (Sep, closed)
```

The timeline reveals a clear pattern: **the foundational chemistry limitations (#152, #189) have been open the longest** -- nearly two years -- while **hardware compatibility issues accumulate as the user base expands beyond H100/A100 environments**. The most recent wave of issues (August-September 2026) focuses on correctness (#730), usability (#732, #714), and GPU diversity (#735, #742).

**Three structural observations:**

1. **The H100/A100 mono-culture is a liability.** Google DeepMind internally runs on TPUs and a narrow set of NVIDIA data-center GPUs. The open-source release exposes a much wider hardware surface, and issues like #735 (segfault on Blackwell) and #742 (autotuning regression on A6000) show that JAX/XLA compatibility with non-target GPUs is poorly tested. The [v3.0.4 Apple Silicon support](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/85c4d20505fd5cef05eac22b534d4e793971ae69) is a positive signal but doesn't address the NVIDIA workstation gap.

2. **Chemistry support is the long pole in the tent.** Bond orders, polymer-polymer covalent bonds, and glycosidic torsion constraints are not edge cases for structural biology -- they are central to drug design and glycobiology. The fact that these issues remain open after 18+ months suggests they require architectural changes to the model or output pipeline, not just bug fixes.
