3. **The feedback loop is slow.** Many well-articulated issues (#675 on redundant featurization, #732 on preflight validation, #609 on runtime discrepancy) receive no maintainer response for months. Community PRs like [#704](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/704) (RNA sequence fix), [#705](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/705) (resource leak fix), [#706](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/706) (compilation buckets), and [#699](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/699) (Apple Silicon GPU) are eventually absorbed into internal commits with "Inspired by" acknowledgments, but the latency between community contribution and integration is measured in weeks to months. This is consistent with Google's internal-first development workflow (PiperOrigin-RevId commits), but it can be demotivating for external contributors.

# About Contributors



AlphaFold 3 is not a community patchwork — it is, at its core, a Google DeepMind product. But looking at who actually ships the code, reviews the PRs, and shepherds the releases reveals a surprisingly lean operation for a project with this much scientific impact. This page takes you behind the curtain: who are the people committing, what is their background, and how does the external contributor ecosystem actually function?

## The Primary Maintainer: Augustin Žídek

If you have interacted with the [google-deepmind/alphafold3](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3) repository in any capacity — filed an issue, read a commit log, or waited for a release — you have encountered **Augustin Žídek**. He is the dominant presence in the commit history, responsible for virtually every recent change landing on `main`.

### Career Timeline

Žídek has been at DeepMind since 2017, making him one of the longest-tenured members of the protein folding team. His trajectory mirrors the evolution of AlphaFold itself:

| Period | Role | Focus |
|--------|------|-------|
| 2017–2021 | Research Engineer | Joined the protein folding team; early AlphaFold research |
| 2021–2024 | Senior Research Engineer | AlphaFold-Multimer, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database |
| 2024–Present | Staff Research Engineer | AlphaFold 3 inference pipeline, open-source releases |

```mermaid
timeline
    title Augustin Žídek at DeepMind
    2017 : Joins DeepMind as Research Engineer on protein folding team
    2020 : AlphaFold 2 breakthrough at CASP14
    2021 : Promoted to Senior Research Engineer; works on AlphaFold-Multimer
    2022 : Helps establish AlphaFold Protein Structure Database "(200M+ structures)"
    2024 : Promoted to Staff Research Engineer; AlphaFold 3 paper published in Nature
    2024 Nov : AlphaFold 3 code released for academic use
    2025 : AlphaFold 3 re-licensed under Apache 2.0 (v3.0.3)
    2025 Jul : Ships CPU-only support and Apple Silicon GPU backend (v3.0.4)
```

On his [personal website](https://augustin.zidek.eu), Žídek describes himself succinctly:

> "I am a Staff Research Engineer working at DeepMind on AlphaFold – computational protein folding. **I enjoy working at the edge of research and engineering.**"

That last sentence is telling. The AlphaFold 3 open-source repo is fundamentally an **engineering** artifact — inference pipeline, data pipeline, Docker setup, CLI flags — not a research artifact. Žídek sits exactly at the seam where the research model meets production infrastructure, which is why his name is on nearly every commit.

### Research Beyond AlphaFold

Žídek's contributions are not limited to protein folding. His publication record on [alphaXiv](https://www.alphaxiv.org/@augustin-zidek) reveals a researcher with genuine breadth:

- **Transfer in Deep Reinforcement Learning Using Successor Features and Generalised Policy Improvement** — extending the SFs & GPI framework for transfer across RL tasks, published at ICML 2019 ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.08860))
- **Kickstarting Deep Reinforcement Learning** — using pre-trained teacher agents to accelerate student training via policy distillation, published at ICLR 2018 ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.03835))
- **Unicorn: Continual Learning with a Universal, Off-policy Agent** — an architecture for continual learning without explicit task boundaries, published at ICML 2018 ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.08240))
- **AlphaQubit 2: A scalable and real-time neural decoder for topological quantum codes** — a neural-network decoder for quantum error correction on surface and color codes, Dec 2025

He also contributed to data infrastructure for structural biology, including the **3D-Beacons network** and **ModelCIF** for representing computed structure models — unglamorous but critical standards work that makes AlphaFold outputs interoperable with the broader PDB ecosystem.

### Public Presence and Release Advocacy

Žídek is the public-facing voice for AlphaFold 3 releases. On LinkedIn, he personally announced both major recent releases:

- **[v3.0.3](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/augustinzidek_release-alphafold-v303-google-deepmind-activity-7470089766227648512-ITkY)** — the Apache 2.0 relicensing, with 416 reactions and community questions about training code
- **[v3.0.4](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/augustinzidek_release-alphafold-v304-google-deepmind-activity-7487915741766344704-mp9J)** — CPU-only support and Apple Silicon GPU, with 728 reactions. His post read: *"I really like this release because you can now run AlphaFold 3 on machines without a GPU, using only the CPU. It is slow, but you no longer need fancy hardware to fold."*

The v3.0.4 announcement drew a notably thoughtful comment from Gianluca Mondillo, MD:

> "This is a genuinely meaningful accessibility release. CPU-only support will not make AlphaFold 3 lightweight or suitable for high-throughput work, but it removes the hard dependency on specialized GPU infrastructure. That matters for teaching, prototyping, reproducibility and smaller labs that need occasional local runs."

## The Broader DeepMind Team

While Žídek is the primary committer visible in the public repository, AlphaFold 3 is the product of a much larger team. The [Nature paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07487-w) lists dozens of authors spanning both **Google DeepMind** and **Isomorphic Labs** (DeepMind's drug discovery spinoff). The key architectural contributions include:

- **The Evoformer trunk** — an improved version of the deep learning architecture from AlphaFold 2
- **The diffusion module** — replacing the structure module of AF2 with a diffusion network that converges from a cloud of atoms to the final structure
- **The confidence head** — predicting per-atom pLDDT scores and the predicted aligned error (PAE)

These research contributions were made by the internal team; the open-source repository primarily exposes the **inference pipeline** that wraps these trained components.

## Hana Joo: Internal Tooling Contributions

The only other committer visible in recent history is **Hana Joo** ([GitHub: h-joo](https://github.com/h-joo)), who authored a commit on 2026-07-26 adding ["Suppressions for pyrefly"](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/01bd8d1f816a95fbf0528e51fa5debabea4f9e69). Pyrefly is an internal Python type-checking tool used at Google. This commit is characteristic of internal infrastructure maintenance — the kind of invisible work that keeps the codebase passing CI in Google's monorepo before it gets exported to GitHub via Piper.

Hana Joo's presence illustrates an important structural fact: **the public GitHub repo is a downstream export of Google's internal monorepo**. Every commit message contains a `PiperOrigin-RevId` and a `Change-Id`, which are Gerrit/Piper identifiers. The contributors you see on GitHub are those whose internal changes happened to be exported in the most recent sync window. The actual set of people working on the code internally is larger.

## External Contributors: The "Inspired By" Pipeline

This is where the contributor story gets structurally interesting. The AlphaFold 3 repo operates under a model where **external contributions are typically absorbed as inspiration rather than merged directly**. The commit messages are remarkably transparent about this:

| Commit | What Changed | External Contributor |
|--------|-------------|---------------------|
| [85c4d2](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/85c4d20505fd5cef05eac22b534d4e793971ae69) | Apple Silicon GPU support (~3x faster on M3) | @SuhasSrinivasan via [PR #699](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/699) |
| [501f7a](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/501f7a9056f1ce20580c45ce588a9a4a4a01dc1b) | Better error when binary not found | @Ayush7614 via [PR #705](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/705) |
| [039eb5](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/039eb598b4bbe773b0d434769a963b777a5522cc) | Don't leak resources when sharded Jackhmmer errors | Inspired by [PR #705](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/705) |
| [29596b](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/29596b97021cfc941b1993249969c4f268efdbab) | Compilation buckets of size 128 and 384 for small proteins | @teerthsharma via [PR #706](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/706) |
| [254614](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/25461454b174c2a21f509554c086bd3c26e8e06a) | Fix loading empty template maps from AF < 3.0.4 | Via [PR #710](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/710) |
| [97d202](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/commit/97d20234c6eb89e8d05376e9eecc9321e60a559b) | Use original RNA sequence in fill_missing_fields | Via [PR #704](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/704) |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[External PR<br/>submitted] --> B{Internal review<br/>by DeepMind}
    B -->|Adapt & rewrite| C[Internal Piper commit<br/>with attribution]
    C --> D[Export to GitHub<br/>with 'Inspired by' note]
    B -->|Reject| E[PR remains open<br/>or closed]
    
    style A fill:#e1f5fe
    style C fill:#c8e6c9
    style D fill:#c8e6c9
    style E fill:#ffcdd2
```

This pattern — **acknowledging the external contributor in the commit message but implementing the change internally** — is a deliberate consequence of Google's Piper/Mercurial workflow. External PRs cannot be directly merged into the internal monorepo; they must be reimplemented internally, and the result is then exported back to GitHub. The commit messages consistently credit the original author ("thanks @username!"), which is transparent but also means **the contributor's name won't appear in GitHub's contributor graph**.

This is a structural tension. The project accepts community improvements, but the mechanics of Google's monorepo make true collaborative development impossible. Contributors like **@SuhasSrinivasan** (Apple Silicon GPU), **@Ayush7614** (resource leak fixes), and **@teerthsharma** (compilation bucket sizes) have materially improved the project, yet their GitHub profiles won't show these contributions.

## Notable Community Contributors

Several external developers have made significant impact through issues and PRs:

- **@SuhasSrinivasan** — Proposed [Apple Silicon GPU support via JAX-MPS](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/699), which was adapted and shipped in v3.0.4. This was one of the most impactful community contributions, delivering roughly **3x faster inference** on MacBook Pro M3 compared to CPU-only mode.

- **@Ayush7614** — Submitted [PR #705](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/705) improving error handling and resource cleanup in the subprocess utilities. Two separate commits were inspired by this single PR.

- **@teerthsharma** — Proposed [PR #706](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/pull/706) adding smaller compilation buckets (128 and 384 tokens) to make running small proteins faster by default, avoiding the overhead of the standard 512-token bucket.

## The Research-to-Engineering Pipeline

Understanding the contributor structure of AlphaFold 3 requires understanding how Google DeepMind works internally. The people who designed the diffusion module, the atom cross-attention layers, and the pair representation are **research scientists**. The person who packages all of that into a runnable pipeline, handles the CLI flags, fixes the subprocess resource leaks, and shepherds the Apache 2.0 relicensing is **Augustin Žídek** — a research engineer.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Research
        R1[Model Architecture<br/>Evoformer, Diffusion Head]
        R2[Training Pipeline<br/>Internal-only]
        R3[Model Weights<br/>Released under CC-BY 4.0]
    end
    
    subgraph Engineering
        E1["Inference Pipeline<br/>run_alphafold.py()"]
        E2[Data Pipeline<br/>MSA, Templates, Featurisation]
        E3["Infrastructure<br/>Docker, JAX backends, C++ bindings"]
    end
    
    subgraph Community
        C1["Issue Reports<br/>~740 open issues"]
        C2[PR Submissions<br/>Adapted internally]
        C3[Usage Feedback<br/>Performance, edge cases]
    end
    
    R1 --> E1
    R2 --> R3
    R3 --> E1
    E1 --> C1
    C2 --> E1
    C3 --> E2
    
    style R1 fill:#e8eaf6
    style R2 fill:#e8eaf6
    style R3 fill:#e8eaf6
    style E1 fill:#c8e6c9
    style E2 fill:#c8e6c9
    style E3 fill:#c8e6c9
    style C1 fill:#fff3e0
    style C2 fill:#fff3e0
    style C3 fill:#fff3e0
```

This division of labor is standard at DeepMind but creates a public-perception problem: the open-source repository appears to be a one-person project, when in reality a large internal team produced the model architecture, trained the weights, and maintains the internal codebase. Žídek is the **bridge** — the person who translates internal research artifacts into external engineering artifacts.

## What This Means for Contributors

If you are considering contributing to AlphaFold 3, understand the structural reality:

1. **Your PR will likely be "inspired by" rather than directly merged.** This is not a value judgment — it is a consequence of Piper. Your contribution will be credited in commit messages but not in GitHub's contributor stats.

2. **The most impactful contributions are ones that address real operational pain points** — resource leaks, better error messages, hardware support (like Apple Silicon), performance tuning for non-standard GPU sizes. These are the changes most likely to be adapted internally because they don't require changes to the model architecture.

3. **The project has a healthy issue culture.** Žídek is responsive to well-structured issues, and the commit log shows that community-reported problems (like the [Haiku version bump for #715](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold3/issues/715)) do get addressed. The bottleneck is the internal review and export cycle, not indifference.

4. **Training code and training infrastructure are not part of this repository** and likely never will be, given Isomorphic Labs' commercial interests in drug discovery. This was [explicitly acknowledged](https://fraserlab.com/2024/05/22/AlphaFold3) during the initial controversy around the delayed code release.

---

The contributor story of AlphaFold 3 is, at its heart, a story about the gap between open-source *code* and open-source *development*. The code is Apache 2.0. The weights are CC-BY 4.0. But the development process is Google-internal, and the bridge between those worlds is one Staff Research Engineer who genuinely seems to enjoy the work.

# Architecture Overview



AlphaFold 3 represents a fundamental architectural redesign from its predecessor, replacing the structure module with a **score-based diffusion model** and introducing **per-atom cross attention** as a first-class mechanism for bridging token-level and atom-level representations. The system is built on **JAX + Haiku** for differentiable computation, with Triton flash attention via `tokamax` for GPU efficiency. This page provides a structural map of the entire pipeline—from JSON input through data processing, neural network inference, and post-processing to final mmCIF output—so you can navigate the codebase with precision.

Sources: [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L1-L200), [model.py](/src/alphafold3/model/model.py#L1-L200)

## End-to-End Pipeline Architecture

The full prediction pipeline executes in three sequential stages, each independently controllable via CLI flags (`--run_data_pipeline`, `--run_inference`):

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input["1. Input Parsing"]
        JSON["JSON Input<br/>(folding_input)"]
    end

    subgraph DataPipeline["2. Data Pipeline"]
        direction TB
        MSA["MSA Search<br/>(Jackhmmer + Nhmmer)"]
        TPL["Template Search<br/>(Hmmsearch + Hmmalign)"]
        FEAT["Featurisation<br/>(WholePdbPipeline)"]
        MSA --> FEAT
        TPL --> FEAT
    end

    subgraph Inference["3. Neural Network Inference"]
        direction TB
        EVO["Evoformer Trunk<br/>(48 PairFormer layers<br/>+ recycling ×10)"]
        DIF["Diffusion Head<br/>(200-step denoising<br/>×5 samples)"]
        CON["Confidence Head<br/>(4 PairFormer layers)"]
        DIS["Distogram Head"]
        EVO --> DIF
        EVO --> CON
        EVO --> DIS
    end

    subgraph Output["4. Post-Processing"]
        POST["mmCIF + Confidences<br/>+ Ranking Score"]
    end

    JSON --> DataPipeline --> Inference --> Output
```

The orchestrator `ModelRunner` in [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L462-L510) JIT-compiles the entire forward pass via `jax.jit`, loads parameters through `params.get_model_haiku_params`, and dispatches to the appropriate JAX device. Each RNG seed produces independent diffusion samples, and results are ranked by a composite confidence score.

Sources: [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L462-L510), [model.py](/src/alphafold3/model/model.py#L230-L330)

## Project Structure Map

```
src/alphafold3/
├── common/                  # Shared abstractions
│   ├── folding_input.py     #   Input JSON → Python data model
│   ├── base_config.py       #   Auto-creating config dataclasses
│   └── resources.py         #   Resource path resolution
├── constants/               # Chemistry constants
│   ├── chemical_components.py  # CCD (Chemical Component Dictionary)
│   ├── atom_types.py        #   Atom type definitions
│   └── residue_names.py     #   Residue name constants
├── data/                    # Data pipeline (MSA + templates + featurisation)
│   ├── pipeline.py          #   MSA/template orchestration per chain
│   ├── featurisation.py     #   Top-level featurise_input()
│   ├── msa.py               #   MSA data class + merging
│   ├── msa_features.py      #   MSA → feature arrays
│   ├── templates.py         #   Template search + realignment
│   └── tools/               #   External tool wrappers (jackhmmer, nhmmer, etc.)
├── model/                   # Neural network core
│   ├── model.py             #   Model class: recycling loop + head dispatch
│   ├── model_config.py      #   GlobalConfig (bfloat16, flash attn, sharding)
│   ├── features.py          #   Feature definitions + BatchDict
│   ├── feat_batch.py        #   Batch dataclass with atom layout info
│   ├── post_processing.py   #   mmCIF output + confidence serialization
│   ├── network/             #   All network modules
│   │   ├── evoformer.py     #     Evoformer trunk (PairFormer + MSA + templates)
│   │   ├── diffusion_head.py#     Score-based diffusion for atom positions
│   │   ├── atom_cross_attention.py  #  Per-atom cross attention encoder/decoder
│   │   ├── confidence_head.py#    Confidence prediction (pLDDT, PAE, pTM)
│   │   ├── diffusion_transformer.py #  Transformer with Adaptive LayerNorm
│   │   ├── modules.py       #     PairFormerIteration, TriangleMult, OuterProduct
│   │   ├── template_modules.py  #  Template embedding
│   │   └── distogram_head.py#    Distogram prediction
│   └── pipeline/            #   Model-side featurisation pipeline
│       ├── pipeline.py      #     WholePdbPipeline (structure → features)
│       └── structure_cleaning.py  #  Structure sanitization
├── structure/               # Structure I/O (mmCIF parsing/writing)
├── jax/geometry/            #   JAX-native rigid body geometry
└── parsers/                 #   C++ accelerated parsers (via pybind11)
```

Sources: [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L37-L55), [model.py](/src/alphafold3/model/model.py#L25-L38)

## Stage 1: Data Pipeline

The data pipeline is orchestrated by [pipeline.py](/src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py) and runs **MSA search** and **template search** per chain in parallel using `ThreadPoolExecutor` (sub-shelled tools bypass the GIL). Protein chains query UniRef90, MGnify, and SmallBFD via **Jackhmmer**, plus UniProt for paired MSA; RNA chains query NT-RNA, Rfam, and RNAcentral via **Nhmmer**. Template search uses **Hmmsearch** against the PDB with date filtering. All results are deduplicated and merged before passing to featurisation.

| Component | Tool | Database(s) | Chain Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unpaired MSA | Jackhmmer | UniRef90, MGnify, SmallBFD | Protein |
| Paired MSA | Jackhmmer | UniProt | Protein |
| Template Search | Hmmsearch + Hmmalign | PDB | Protein |
| RNA MSA | Nhmmer | NT-RNA, Rfam, RNAcentral | RNA |

> [!TIP]
> The data pipeline results are cached per sequence via `@functools.cache`, so identical sequences in homomers do not trigger redundant searches.

Sources: [pipeline.py](/src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L40-L155)

## Stage 2: Featurisation and Batching

The `WholePdbPipeline` in [model/pipeline/pipeline.py](/src/alphafold3/model/pipeline/pipeline.py#L103-L200) converts the cleaned structure, MSAs, and templates into a `BatchDict` of NumPy arrays. Key responsibilities include: structure cleaning (hydrogen removal, leaving-atom filtering, glycan handling), tokenisation (each residue becomes a token with up to **24 atom slots**), MSA cropping (max 16,384 sequences), template featurisation (max 4 templates), inter-chain bond computation, and bucket-based padding to avoid JIT recompilation. The Chemical Component Dictionary (CCD) provides reference conformers for ligands via RDKit.

Sources: [pipeline.py](/src/alphafold3/model/pipeline/pipeline.py#L103-L200), [featurisation.py](/src/alphafold3/data/featurisation.py#L43-L122)

## Stage 3: Neural Network Core

The `Model.__call__` method in [model.py](/src/alphafold3/model/model.py#L280-L330) implements the full forward pass with three sub-stages executed sequentially:

### 3.1 Evoformer Trunk

The Evoformer ([evoformer.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/evoformer.py)) is the central representation-learning engine. It produces two outputs: a **single embedding** (per-token, 384 channels) and a **pair embedding** (token-pair, 128 channels). Internally it executes:

1. **Target feature embedding** — one-hot residue features concatenated with per-atom conditioning from `atom_cross_att_encoder`
2. **Sequence-pair embedding** — outer product of single projections forming initial pair activations
3. **Relative position encoding** — relative index and chain encodings added to pair
4. **Bond embedding** — polymer-ligand and ligand-ligand bond contact matrices projected into pair space
5. **Template embedding** — intra-chain template features processed through a template stack
6. **MSA stack** — EvoformerIteration (MSA attention + outer product mean + triangle multiplication) updating both MSA and pair representations
7. **PairFormer stack** — **48 layers** of `PairFormerIteration`, each containing:
   - Pair attention (with pair bias, gated)
   - Single attention (with pair bias)
   - Triangle multiplication (outgoing + incoming)
   - Triangle attention (starting + ending)
   - Single transition + Pair transition

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Evoformer["Evoformer Trunk"]
        direction TB
        TFE["Target Feat +<br/>Atom Cross Att Encoder"]
        SEQ["Seq-Pair Embedding"]
        REL["Relative Encoding"]
        BND["Bond Embedding"]
        TPL["Template Embedding"]
        MSA_S["MSA Stack<br/>(EvoformerIteration)"]
        PF["PairFormer ×48 layers"]

        TFE --> SEQ --> REL --> BND --> TPL --> MSA_S --> PF
    end

    PF -->|single: N×384| OUT_S["Single Embedding"]
    PF -->|pair: N×N×128| OUT_P["Pair Embedding"]
```

### 3.2 Recycling Loop

The Evoformer trunk is wrapped in a **recycling loop** (default 10 recycles) implemented via `hk.fori_loop` for JAX compatibility. On the first pass, single and pair embeddings are zero-initialized. On subsequent passes, the previous cycle's embeddings are fed back as `prev` inputs, allowing the model to iteratively refine its representations. This is the critical mechanism that enables progressive improvement of predictions.

### 3.3 Diffusion Head

The Diffusion Head ([diffusion_head.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/diffusion_head.py)) replaces AlphaFold 2's structure module entirely. It generates atom coordinates through **score-based denoising diffusion**:

- **Conditioning**: Single and pair embeddings from the trunk are projected and augmented with relative encodings and noise-level embeddings
- **Atom Cross Attention Encoder**: Converts token-level conditioning into per-atom queries using reference structure (positions, elements, charges, atom names)
- **Denoising Transformer**: A 24-block Transformer with Adaptive LayerNorm (AdaLN-Zero) processes atom-level representations
- **Atom Cross Attention Decoder**: Maps per-atom outputs back to token space
- **Sampling**: 200 denoising steps with noise schedule σ(t), producing **5 independent samples** by default

The noise schedule follows σ(t) = σ_data · (s_max^(1/p) + t·(s_min^(1/p) − s_max^(1/p)))^p with σ_data=16.0, p=7. Random rigid augmentations (rotation + translation) are applied during training for SE(3) equivariance.

### 3.4 Confidence Head

The Confidence Head ([confidence_head.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/confidence_head.py)) runs **after** diffusion sampling, evaluating all 5 samples. It uses a lightweight **4-layer PairFormer** to refine the pair representation with distance features from predicted atom positions, then outputs:

| Output | Description | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| pLDDT | Per-atom predicted LDDT confidence | (N_atoms,) |
| PAE | Predicted Aligned Error (token-pair) | (N_tokens, N_tokens) |
| pTM | Predicted TM-score (global) | scalar |
| ipTM | Interface pTM (chain-pair) | scalar |

### 3.5 Distogram Head

A lightweight head that produces a token-level distogram from the pair embeddings, useful for downstream analysis but not used for structure generation.

Sources: [model.py](/src/alphafold3/model/model.py#L230-L330), [evoformer.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/evoformer.py#L33-L115), [diffusion_head.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/diffusion_head.py#L33-L110), [confidence_head.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/confidence_head.py#L33-L85)

## Neural Network Architecture Summary

| Component | Layers | Key Dimensions | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Evoformer PairFormer | 48 | single: 384, pair: 128 | Single + Pair embeddings |
| Evoformer MSA Stack | configurable | msa: 64 | Updated MSA + Pair |
| Diffusion Transformer | 24 blocks | AdaLN-Zero | Atom positions |
| Confidence PairFormer | 4 | Reuses trunk dims | pLDDT, PAE, pTM |
| Recycling | 10 iterations | — | Refined embeddings |
| Diffusion Sampling | 200 steps × 5 samples | σ_data=16 | 5 candidate structures |

Sources: [evoformer.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/evoformer.py#L50-L80), [diffusion_transformer.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/diffusion_transformer.py#L1-L50), [model_config.py](/src/alphafold3/model/model_config.py#L27-L44)

## Stage 4: Post-Processing and Output

Post-processing in [post_processing.py](/src/alphafold3/model/post_processing.py#L60-L110) converts each `InferenceResult` into final output files. Atom coordinates are rearranged from the model's internal layout to the flat output layout via `atom_layout.convert`, then assembled into a `Structure` object with B-factors set to pLDDT scores. The pipeline produces:

- **`model.cif`** — mmCIF file with predicted coordinates, B-factors, and metadata
- **`confidences.json`** — Full confidence data (pLDDT, PAE, pTM, ipTM, ranking score)
- **`summary_confidences.json`** — Summary confidence metrics

Multiple samples are ranked by a composite `ranking_score`, and the best-ranked sample is typically used as the final prediction.

Sources: [post_processing.py](/src/alphafold3/model/post_processing.py#L60-L110), [model.py](/src/alphafold3/model/model.py#L80-L130)

## Infrastructure and Acceleration

The system employs several key infrastructure choices for performance:

| Technology | Purpose | Configuration |
|---|---|---|
| **JAX + Haiku** | Differentiable computation, JIT compilation | `jax.jit` on full forward pass |
| **Bfloat16** | Reduced-precision computation | `global_config.bfloat16 = 'all'` |
| **Triton Flash Attention** | Memory-efficient attention | `tokamax` with `flash_attention_implementation = 'triton'` |
| **tokamax GLU kernel** | Fused Gated Linear Unit | Used in TransitionBlock, TriangleMult |
| **C++ pybind11** | Fast parsers and MSA profiling | `cpp.cc`, `parsers/cpp/`, `data/cpp/` |
| **Sharded inference** | Memory-efficient batched diffusion | `mapping.sharded_map` for confidence head |
| **Gradient remat** | Recomputation vs. memory trade-off | `block_remat` in PairFormer |

> [!TIP]
> The `ModelRunner` caches both model parameters (`@functools.cached_property`) and the JIT-compiled forward pass, so repeated predictions on the same device reuse the compiled XLA program without recompilation.

Sources: [model_config.py](/src/alphafold3/model/model_config.py#L27-L44), [run_alphafold.py](/run_alphafold.py#L483-L503)

## What's Different from AlphaFold 2

| Aspect | AlphaFold 2 | AlphaFold 3 |
|---|---|---|
| Structure generation | IPA (Invariant Point Attention) module | Score-based diffusion model |
| Molecule types | Proteins only | Proteins, RNA, DNA, ligands, ions |
| Attention at atom level | None (residue-centric) | Atom Cross Attention (encoder + decoder) |
| Recycling | 3 recycles | 10 recycles |
| Confidence | single pLDDT + PAE | pLDDT + PAE + pTM + ipTM + ranking |
| Template usage | Per-chain templates | Per-chain templates with bond embedding |
| Framework | JAX + Haiku | JAX + Haiku (same, extended) |
| Flash attention | None | Triton via tokamax |

Sources: [diffusion_head.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/diffusion_head.py#L33-L110), [atom_cross_attention.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/atom_cross_attention.py#L1-L50), [evoformer.py](/src/alphafold3/model/network/evoformer.py#L50-L80)

To deepen your understanding of specific subsystems, follow this reading path:

1. **[MSA Search Pipeline](8-msa-search-pipeline)** — How Jackhmmer and Nhmmer construct multiple sequence alignments
2. **[Template Search](9-template-search)** — How Hmmsearch finds and realigns structural templates
3. **[Featurisation and Batching](10-featurisation-and-batching)** — How raw data becomes model-ready feature arrays

8. **[Output Format and Metrics](15-output-format-and-metrics)** — mmCIF structure and confidence score interpretation

# MSA Search Pipeline



The MSA (Multiple Sequence Alignment) Search Pipeline is AlphaFold 3's evolutionary intelligence layer — the stage where query sequences are matched against massive biological databases to uncover homologous relationships. These alignments encode the co-evolutionary signals that the Evoformer trunk later exploits to infer structural contacts. The pipeline orchestrates two distinct HMMER-family tools across seven specialised databases, merges results with deduplication, and produces featurised arrays ready for the neural network.

## Architecture Overview

The MSA search pipeline follows a **per-chain dispatch pattern**: protein chains are routed to Jackhmmer against four databases, while RNA chains are routed to Nhmmer against three databases. Both paths execute database queries in parallel via `ThreadPoolExecutor`, merge and deduplicate results, then hand off to the featurisation stage.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input
        QC[Query Chain]
    end

    subgraph Dispatch
        QC -->|Protein| PP[Protein MSA Path]
        QC -->|RNA| RP[RNA MSA Path]
    end

    subgraph Protein Parallel
        PP --> J1[Jackhmmer<br/>UniRef90]
        PP --> J2[Jackhmmer<br/>MGnify]
        PP --> J3[Jackhmmer<br/>smallBFD]
        PP --> J4[Jackhmmer<br/>UniProt]
    end

    subgraph RNA Parallel
        RP --> N1[Nhmmer<br/>NT-RNA]
        RP --> N2[Nhmmer<br/>Rfam]
        RP --> N3[Nhmmer<br/>RNAcentral]
    end

    subgraph Merge
        J1 & J2 & J3 --> UMSA[Unpaired MSA<br/>Deduplicate=True]
        J4 --> PMSA[Paired MSA<br/>Deduplicate=False]
        N1 & N2 & N3 --> RMSA[RNA MSA<br/>Deduplicate=True]
    end

    subgraph Output
        UMSA --> FEAT[Featurised Arrays<br/>msa + deletion_matrix<br/>+ species_identifiers]
        PMSA --> FEAT
        RMSA --> FEAT
    end
```

The **unpaired MSA** (UniRef90 + smallBFD + MGnify) captures diverse evolutionary depth. The **paired MSA** (UniProt cluster annotations) captures co-evolution between chains that appear together in the same organism — a critical signal for multimeric complex prediction. RNA chains produce a single merged MSA since pairing logic is not applicable.

Sources: [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L80-L161), [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L166-L210)

## Tool Dispatch and the MsaTool Protocol

Both Jackhmmer and Nhmmer conform to the `MsaTool` protocol — a minimal interface requiring a single `query(target_sequence) → MsaToolResult` method. The `get_msa_tool` factory function uses Python's `match` statement to instantiate the correct tool from the config type, and `get_msa` orchestrates the full query-to-`Msa` object lifecycle.

| Component | Responsibility | Key Method |
|---|---|---|
| `MsaTool` (Protocol) | Interface contract for all MSA tools | `query(target_sequence) → MsaToolResult` |
| `MsaToolResult` | Immutable result container | Holds `a3m`, `e_value`, `target_sequence`, `tblout` |
| `get_msa_tool()` | Factory dispatching config → tool instance | Pattern matches `JackhmmerConfig` / `NhmmerConfig` |
| `get_msa()` | End-to-end: tool query → `Msa` construction | Calls `Msa.from_a3m()` with crop and dedup |

The `MsaToolResult` dataclass carries both the alignment in **A3M format** (uppercase residues + lowercase insertions) and an optional `tblout` string containing tabular hit statistics — needed only when merging results across sharded databases.

Sources: [msa_tool.py](src/alphafold3/data/tools/msa_tool.py#L26-L48), [msa.py](src/alphafold3/data/msa.py#L296-L356)

## Jackhmmer: Protein MSA Search

**Jackhmmer** is an iterative profile HMM search tool from the HMMER3 suite. AlphaFold 3 runs it against **four protein databases** simultaneously using a `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4)`, sidestepping the GIL since the tool is sub-shelled out as an external process.

### Protein Database Configuration

| Database | Tool | E-value | Max Sequences | Role | MSA Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| UniRef90 | Jackhmmer | 1e-4 | 10,000 | Primary diverse homologs; feeds template search | Unpaired |
| smallBFD | Jackhmmer | 1e-4 | 5,000 | Broad fold-level diversity | Unpaired |
| MGnify | Jackhmmer | 1e-4 | 5,000 | Metagenomic sequences (novel folds) | Unpaired |
| UniProt Cluster Annot | Jackhmmer | 1e-4 | 50,000 | Inter-chain co-evolution (paired MSA) | Paired |

All four Jackhmmer instances use `n_iter=1` — a single search pass rather than the default iterative refinement. This is a deliberate trade-off: iterative searches are slower and can amplify noise, while the large database breadth compensates for the reduced per-database depth.

### Sharded Database Execution

When a database path contains a shard specifier (e.g. `<db_path>@<num_shards>`), Jackhmmer runs each shard as a separate subprocess in parallel. The `Z-value` and `domZ-value` must be set to the full (unsharded) database size to ensure e-values are correctly scaled across shards. Results are merged via `_merge_jackhmmer_results`, which:

1. Parses the `tblout` from each shard to extract per-hit e-values and bit scores
2. Creates a lazy iterator over each shard's A3M, cross-referencing with tblout data
3. Merges all iterators via `heapq.merge` sorted by `(e-value, -bit_score, name)`
4. Truncates to `max_sequences`, preserving the top-scoring hits globally

> [!TIP]
> Sharded search results may contain near-duplicates that Jackhmmer's internal deduplication cannot detect across shard boundaries. This is intentional and bounded — the downstream `Msa` deduplication step cleans these up.

Sources: [jackhmmer.py](src/alphafold3/data/tools/jackhmmer.py#L37-L196), [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L309-L382)

## Nhmmer: RNA MSA Search

**Nhmmer** performs profile HMM search against nucleotide databases, specialised for RNA sequence alignment. Unlike Jackhmmer, Nhmmer requires a **two-step alignment process** because its hits are typically shorter than the query sequence:

1. **Search**: Nhmmer queries the database, producing Stockholm-format hits
2. **Profile alignment**: `hmmbuild` constructs a profile HMM from the query, then `hmmalign` re-aligns Nhmmer's hits against this full-length profile

This ensures the output MSA has consistent width matching the query sequence — a requirement for downstream featurisation.

### RNA Database Configuration

| Database | Tool | E-value | Max Sequences | Alphabet |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NT-RNA | Nhmmer | 1e-3 | 10,000 | rna |
| Rfam | Nhmmer | 1e-3 | 10,000 | rna |
| RNAcentral | Nhmmer | 1e-3 | 10,000 | rna |

Nhmmer applies a **relaxed F3 filter** (0.02) for short RNA sequences (< 50 residues), as recommended by RNAcentral — the default aggressive filtering would discard many valid short-RNA hits. Sharded merging follows the same `heapq.merge` strategy as Jackhmmer, but uses column 12 (e-value) from nucleotide tblout format rather than column 5.

Sources: [nhmmer.py](src/alphafold3/data/tools/nhmmer.py#L43-L300), [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L383-L439)

## Msa Container: Deduplication and Merging

The `Msa` class is the central data structure — a validated, optionally deduplicated container for alignment sequences and their descriptions. It enforces a critical invariant: **the first sequence must be feature-equivalent to the query sequence**, verified via `_featurize` which maps residues through the same encoding used by the neural network.

### Deduplication Strategy

Deduplication strips lowercase characters (insertions) from each sequence using `str.maketrans` for O(n) performance, then tracks unique uppercase-only sequences in a set. This is applied at two levels:

| Merge Operation | Deduplicate | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Unpaired protein MSA (`from_multiple_msas`) | **True** | UniRef90, smallBFD, and MGnify overlap significantly |
| Paired protein MSA (`from_multiple_msas`) | **False** | UniProt is the sole source; no cross-DB duplicates |
| RNA MSA (`from_multiple_msas`) | **True** | Rfam, RNAcentral, and NT-RNA share entries |

### Construction Pathways

The `Msa` class provides three class methods for different construction scenarios:

- **`from_a3m(query_sequence, chain_poly_type, a3m, max_depth)`** — parses a single A3M string, optionally cropping to `max_depth` sequences
- **`from_multiple_a3ms(a3ms, chain_poly_type)`** — merges multiple raw A3M strings, validating that query sequences match
- **`from_multiple_msas(msas)`** — merges already-constructed `Msa` objects, the primary path used by `DataPipeline`

The empty MSA (`from_empty`) is used when a chain provides pre-computed MSAs or when MSA search is intentionally skipped.

Sources: [msa.py](src/alphafold3/data/msa.py#L61-L262)

## Featurisation: MSA to Neural Network Input

The `Msa.featurize()` method converts the raw sequence alignment into the numerical arrays consumed by the Evoformer. It calls two extraction functions:

**`extract_msa_features(msa_sequences, chain_poly_type)`** produces two arrays of shape `(num_seq, num_res)`:

| Output Array | Content | Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| `msa` | Uppercase residues and gaps | Protein: 0–21 (20 AA + gap), RNA: 22–25 + 21 (gap), DNA: 26–29 + 21 (gap) |
| `deletion_matrix` | Count of lowercase insertions left of each residue | Integer counts |

The encoding is **non-overlapping across polymer types**: protein residues occupy indices 0–20, RNA nucleotides start at 22, and DNA nucleotides at 26 — with gap (`-`) consistently at 21 and unknown nucleic residues at 30. Lowercase characters in the A3M (representing insertions relative to the query) are stripped from the MSA array but their counts are recorded in the deletion matrix.

**`extract_species_ids(msa_descriptions)`** parses UniProtKB-style description headers using a regex matching the pattern `(tr|sp)|Accession|EntryName_SpeciesId`, extracting the 1–5 character species code. Species identifiers enable the pairing algorithm to identify sequences from the same organism across different chains.

Sources: [msa.py](src/alphafold3/data/msa.py#L263-L293), [msa_features.py](src/alphafold3/data/msa_features.py#L80-L169), [msa_features.py](src/alphafold3/data/msa_features.py#L175-L200)

## DataPipeline Orchestration

The `DataPipeline` class wires everything together. Its `__init__` constructs all `RunConfig` objects from `DataPipelineConfig`, and its `process()` method iterates over chains with type-based dispatch:

| Chain Type | Method | MSA Search | Template Search |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ProteinChain` | `process_protein_chain()` | 4× Jackhmmer in parallel | Hmmsearch on UniRef90 MSA |
| `RnaChain` | `process_rna_chain()` | 3× Nhmmer in parallel | Not applicable |

> [!TIP]
> The pipeline uses `@functools.cache` on `_get_protein_msa_and_templates` and `_get_rna_msa` to avoid redundant searches for identical sequences in homomers (e.g., a homodimer with the same chain sequence). This is a significant optimisation for symmetric complexes.

### Pre-computed MSA Handling

The pipeline respects user-supplied MSAs through a three-way branching logic in `process_protein_chain()`:

1. **No MSA provided** → Run full MSA + template search
2. **MSA provided, no templates** → Run template search only (using supplied MSA to build the HMM profile)
3. **Both MSA and templates provided** → Skip all search, use supplied data directly

This enables users to pre-compute MSAs offline (e.g., on a cluster) and supply them at inference time, dramatically reducing runtime for repeated predictions.

Sources: [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L304-L558), [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L591-L610)

## Configuration Reference

The complete MSA search configuration is expressed through frozen dataclasses in `msa_config.py`, ensuring immutability and validation at construction time:

| Config Class | Purpose | Key Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `DatabaseConfig` | Database identity | `name`, `path` |
| `JackhmmerConfig` | Jackhmmer invocation | `binary_path`, `database_config`, `n_cpu`, `n_iter`, `e_value`, `z_value`, `dom_z_value`, `max_sequences`, `max_parallel_shards` |
| `NhmmerConfig` | Nhmmer invocation | `binary_path`, `hmmalign_binary_path`, `hmmbuild_binary_path`, `database_config`, `n_cpu`, `e_value`, `z_value`, `max_sequences`, `alphabet`, `max_parallel_shards` |
| `RunConfig` | Single MSA run | `config` (Jackhmmer or Nhmmer), `chain_poly_type`, `crop_size` |
| `DataPipelineConfig` | Full pipeline | All binary paths, all database paths, Z-values, CPU counts, `max_template_date` |

`RunConfig.__post_init__` validates that `crop_size ≥ 2` (since the query itself always occupies one slot) and that `chain_poly_type` is a recognised standard polymer type.

Sources: [msa_config.py](src/alphafold3/data/msa_config.py#L36-L131), [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L213-L301)

## Key Design Patterns

**Parallel sub-shelling**: Since HMMER tools are external C binaries, they release the GIL. `ThreadPoolExecutor` achieves true parallelism without multiprocessing overhead. Protein chains use `max_workers=4` for the four simultaneous Jackhmmer searches.

**Lazy merging**: The sharded merge functions use `heapq.merge` over lazy iterators — only parsing as many A3M sequences as needed to fill `max_sequences`, avoiding the memory cost of loading all hits from all shards simultaneously.

**Homomer caching**: `@functools.cache` on `_get_protein_msa_and_templates` and `_get_rna_msa` ensures identical sequences in symmetric assemblies trigger a single database search. The cache key is the sequence string itself, so this optimisation is exact for homomers and approximate for near-identical chains.

**Feature-equivalence validation**: The first MSA sequence is validated against the query using the same featurisation pipeline that feeds the neural network, not raw string equality. This accounts for Jackhmmer occasionally mutating residues (e.g., ambiguous codes) while preserving semantic equivalence.

---

**Next steps**: The MSA output flows directly into template search, which uses the UniRef90 alignment to construct an HMM profile for Hmmsearch against the PDB. See [Template Search](9-template-search) for that pipeline, or [Featurisation and Batching](10-featurisation-and-batching) for how the MSA arrays are assembled into model inputs.

# Template Search



Template search is the second stage of AlphaFold 3's data pipeline, responsible for discovering structurally resolved homologs in the PDB and extracting their atomic coordinates as structural priors for the neural network. The pipeline transforms an MSA-derived sequence profile into a set of template features — atom positions, residue types, and ligand coordinates — that the Evoformer trunk can attend to alongside the MSA. This stage operates exclusively on **protein chains**; RNA and DNA chains do not undergo template search in the current implementation.

## Architectural Overview

The template search pipeline comprises four sequential phases: **profile construction**, **database search**, **hit filtering**, and **featurization**. Each phase is orchestrated by the `Templates` class, which serves as the central container and coordinator for all template-related state.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Unpaired Protein MSA<br/>(A3M format)"] --> B["hmmbuild<br/>Profile HMM Construction"]
    B --> C["hmmsearch<br/>PDB seqres Database"]
    C --> D["Raw A3M Hits"]
    D --> E["Hit Parsing &<br/>Metadata Enrichment"]
    E --> F["Hit Filtering<br/>(date, length, ratio, dedup)"]
    F --> G["Structure Retrieval<br/>(mmCIF from StructureStore)"]
    G --> H["Query-to-Hit Mapping<br/>& Realignment"]
    H --> I["Featurization<br/>(atom positions, aatype, ligands)"]
    I --> J["TemplateFeatures<br/>(stacked NumPy arrays)"]

    style A fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#388e3c
    style J fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0
    style F fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#ef6c00
    style H fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#c62828
```

The pipeline is invoked from `DataPipeline` after MSA construction completes. The UniRef90-derived unpaired MSA (in A3M format) serves as the input profile for the template search — this is a deliberate design choice, as UniRef90 provides broad evolutionary coverage that improves HMM sensitivity against the PDB sequence database.

Sources: [pipeline.py](/src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L40-L76), [templates.py](/src/alphafold3/data/templates.py#L438-L492)

## Profile Construction and Database Search

The search begins by converting the unpaired protein MSA into a **Hidden Markov Model (HMM) profile** using HMMer's `hmmbuild` tool. The MSA is first converted from A3M to Stockholm format, which enables reference column annotation — critical for the `--hand` model construction strategy that preserves the query's consensus columns rather than letting `hmmbuild` auto-detect them.

```
A3M MSA → Stockholm → hmmbuild --hand → HMM profile → hmmsearch → A3M hits
```

The `Hmmsearch` wrapper orchestrates this two-step process. It constructs the profile via `Hmmbuild.build_profile_from_sto()` with `model_construction='hand'`, then searches the PDB seqres database (a FASTA file of all PDB chain sequences) using the resulting HMM. The search output is captured in Stockholm format (`-A` flag) and converted back to A3M for downstream parsing.

The `HmmsearchConfig` dataclass exposes fine-grained control over the search:

| Parameter | Default | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `e_value` | (required) | Reporting E-value threshold for inclusion in output |
| `inc_e` | (required) | Inclusion E-value for next-round search |
| `dom_e` | (required) | Domain E-value threshold for reporting |
| `incdom_e` | (required) | Domain E-value for inclusion |
| `n_cpu` | 8 | Number of CPU threads |
| `alphabet` | `'amino'` | HMM alphabet (`amino`, `rna`, `dna`) |
| `filter_f1` / `f2` / `f3` | `None` | MSV, Viterbi, and Forward pre-filter thresholds |
| `filter_max` | `False` | Disables all filters (`--max` flag) |

Setting `filter_max=True` removes all pre-filters, which is slower but avoids missing distant homologs that the cascade filters might discard.

> [!TIP]
> The `max_a3m_query_sequences` parameter (default 300 in `TemplateToolConfig`) limits how many MSA sequences are used to build the HMM profile. This caps computational cost while retaining sufficient evolutionary signal for sensitive searches.

Sources: [hmmsearch.py](/src/alphafold3/data/tools/hmmsearch.py#L31-L162), [hmmbuild.py](/src/alphafold3/data/tools/hmmbuild.py#L61-L77), [templates.py](/src/alphafold3/data/templates.py#L968-L993), [msa_config.py](/src/alphafold3/data/msa_config.py#L133-L176)

## Hit Data Model and Alignment Mapping

Each template hit is represented by the **`Hit` dataclass**, a frozen, slot-optimized container that captures both the search result and its structural metadata:

| Attribute | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `pdb_id` | `str` | Lowercase PDB identifier (e.g., `"4pqx"`) |
| `auth_chain_id` | `str` | Author chain ID from the PDB |
| `hmmsearch_sequence` | `str` | Raw aligned sequence from hmmsearch (uppercase = match, lowercase = deletion, `-` = gap) |
| `structure_sequence` | `str` | Actual sequence from the mmCIF structure |
| `query_sequence` | `str` | The original query sequence |
| `start_index` / `end_index` | `int` | 0-based half-open interval of the hit within the full PDB seqres sequence |
| `full_length` | `int` | Length of the full PDB seqres sequence |
| `release_date` | `datetime.date` | PDB release date |
| `chain_poly_type` | `str` | Polymer type (`protein`, `rna`, `dna`) |
| `unresolved_res_indices` | `Sequence[int]` | 0-based indices of structurally unresolved residues |

The most critical derived property is **`query_to_hit_mapping`**, a `Mapping[int, int]` that maps each query residue index to its corresponding position in the hit structure. This mapping is computed by parsing the hmmsearch A3M alignment encoding:

- **Uppercase residues** → aligned in both query and template (added to mapping)
- **Lowercase residues** → deletions in the template (advance hit index only)
- **Hyphens (`-`)** → insertions in the template (advance query index only)

This mapping is the foundation for all downstream featurization — it determines which template atom positions correspond to which query positions.

Sources: [templates.py](/src/alphafold3/data/templates.py#L166-L306)

## Sequence Realignment

A subtle but important edge case arises when the **PDB seqres sequence** (the theoretical full sequence from the PDB header) differs from the **actual structure sequence** (the sequence extracted from atomic coordinates in the mmCIF). This discrepancy occurs because some residues may lack coordinates due to experimental limitations. When `full_length != len(structure_sequence)`, the original query-to-hit mapping (derived from the seqres sequence) must be **realigned to the actual structure sequence**.

The `realign_hit_to_structure()` function implements a greedy alignment algorithm that:

1. Determines the maximum number of gaps (`full_length - len(structure_sequence)`)
2. Iterates over possible gap placements before the hit subsequence region
3. For each candidate alignment, computes a score (number of matching aligned residues)
4. Selects the alignment with the highest score

The inner `_remap_to_struc_seq()` function walks both sequences simultaneously, shifting the hit index forward when residues don't match (consuming gaps from the budget) and remapping the original query-to-hit indices through the resulting hit-to-structure mapping.

```
Example:
  hit_sequence   : ---DEFGHIJK-    (seqres)
  struc_sequence : --XDEFGH--KL    (actual mmCIF)
  Result mapping : {3:1, 4:2, 5:3, 6:4, 7:5, 10:6}
```

If realignment fails, an `AlignmentError` is raised, and the hit is excluded during filtering.

Sources: [template_realign.py](/src/alphafold3/data/template_realign.py#L29-L177), [templates.py](/src/alphafold3/data/templates.py#L220-L247)

## Hit Filtering Pipeline

Raw hmmsearch results can contain hundreds of hits, many of which are redundant, too recent, or poorly aligned. The `_filter_hits()` function applies a cascading sequence of filters to produce a high-quality, diverse template set:

| Filter | Config Parameter | Logic |
|--------|-----------------|-------|
| **Release date** | `max_template_date` | Excludes hits released after cutoff; prevents ground truth leakage during training |
| **Subsequence ratio** | `max_subsequence_ratio` | Excludes hits where `length_ratio > threshold` AND the hit sequence is an exact subsequence of the query (catches near-duplicates) |
| **Minimum hit length** | `min_hit_length` | Excludes hits with fewer aligned residues than threshold |
| **Validity check** | (automatic) | Excludes hits where all aligned positions map to unresolved residues (`is_valid` property) |
| **Alignment ratio** | `min_align_ratio` | Excludes hits where `align_ratio ≤ threshold` (too few residues aligned relative to query length) |
| **Deduplication** | `deduplicate_sequences` | Keeps only the first hit with a given `output_templates_sequence` |
| **Maximum hits** | `max_hits` | Caps the total number of retained hits |

The **release date cutoff** is computed as `min(max_template_date, query_release_date - 60 days)`. The 60-day buffer (`_DAYS_BEFORE_QUERY_DATE`) provides an additional safety margin against temporal leakage when the query's own release date is known.

Filtering can occur at two points: **eagerly** during `Templates.from_hmmsearch_a3m()` (when `filter_config` is provided), or **lazily** via the `Templates.filter()` method after construction. Eager filtering is more performant because it avoids fetching mmCIF files for hits that will be discarded.

Sources: [templates.py](/src/alphafold3/data/templates.py#L311-L402), [templates.py](/src/alphafold3/data/templates.py#L610-L651), [msa_config.py](/src/alphafold3/data/msa_config.py#L179-L200)

## Structure Retrieval and Featurization

### Structure Store

The `StructureStore` class provides a unified interface for retrieving mmCIF files from three backend types:

| Backend | Initialization | Use Case |
|---------|---------------|----------|
| **Directory** | `StructureStore(path_to_dir/)` | Local filesystem with `{pdb_id}.cif` files |
| **TAR archive** | `StructureStore(path_to.tar)` | Packed mmCIF archive (lazy member index via `@cached_property`) |
| **In-memory mapping** | `StructureStore({"pdb_id": mmcif_string})` | Testing and programmatic use |

If a requested PDB ID is not found, a `NotFoundError` is raised, and the hit is logged as a warning and skipped during parsing.

### Featurization

The `Templates.featurize()` method converts filtered hits into the numerical features consumed by the neural network. For each hit, it:

1. **Retrieves the mmCIF** from the StructureStore (deduplicated by PDB ID — structures shared across multiple hits are loaded once)
2. **Filters to the hit's chain** using `structure.filter(chain_id=label_chain_id)`
3. **Computes polymer features** via `get_polymer_features()`:
   - `template_all_atom_positions`: shape `(query_len, num_atom_types, 3)` — 3D coordinates mapped from hit positions to query positions using `query_to_hit_mapping`
   - `template_all_atom_masks`: shape `(query_len, num_atom_types)` — binary mask indicating which atoms have coordinates
   - `template_aatype`: shape `(query_len,)` — integer-encoded residue types
   - `template_sequence`: the aligned template sequence (with `-` for unaligned positions)
   - `template_domain_names`: hit identifier (e.g., `"4pqx_A"`)
   - `template_release_date`: ISO-format date string

4. **Computes ligand features** (if `include_ligand_features=True`) via `_get_ligand_features()`:
   - `ligand_atom_positions`, `ligand_atom_names`, `ligand_atom_occupancies`, `ccd_id` — per-ligand-chain dictionaries of atom-level data

5. **Stacks all polymer features** across hits using `np.stack(axis=0)`, while ligand features remain as an unstacked list of dictionaries

The polymer-specific atom type count depends on chain type: proteins use 37 atom types (`ATOM37`), while DNA and RNA use 29 (`ATOM29`). The minimum atom count thresholds for validity are 5 for protein, 21 for DNA, and 20 for RNA.

> [!TIP]
> Template featurization is the most I/O-intensive stage because it loads full mmCIF files from disk. Eager filtering (passing `filter_config` to `from_hmmsearch_a3m`) dramatically reduces the number of mmCIF reads by eliminating invalid hits before structure retrieval.

Sources: [structure_stores.py](/src/alphafold3/data/structure_stores.py#L32-L122), [templates.py](/src/alphafold3/data/templates.py#L671-L727), [templates.py](/src/alphafold3/data/templates.py#L829-L954)

## Pipeline Integration

Template search is embedded within `DataPipeline._get_protein_templates()`, which is called from `_get_protein_msa_and_templates()`. The execution order is:

1. **MSA search** runs first (UniRef90, MGnify, SmallBFD, UniProt — in parallel via `ThreadPoolExecutor`)
2. **MSA deduplication** produces the unpaired and paired MSA
3. **Template search** runs on the unpaired MSA's A3M representation

Both `_get_protein_templates` and `_get_protein_msa_and_templates` are decorated with `@functools.cache`, ensuring that identical sequences in homomeric inputs share the same template search results without redundant computation.

When `run_template_search=False`, an empty `Templates` object is constructed with no hits — this allows running AlphaFold 3 in MSA-only mode without external database dependencies.

Sources: [pipeline.py](/src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L39-L161)

## Configuration Reference

The template search pipeline is configured through three nested dataclasses within `msa_config.py`:

| Dataclass | Key Fields | Role |
|-----------|-----------|------|
| `HmmsearchConfig` | `hmmsearch_binary_path`, `hmmbuild_binary_path`, `e_value`, `inc_e`, `dom_e`, `incdom_e`, `alphabet`, `filter_*` | hmmsearch tool parameters |
| `TemplateToolConfig` | `database_path`, `chain_poly_type`, `hmmsearch_config`, `max_a3m_query_sequences` (default 300) | Search target and profile limits |
| `TemplateFilterConfig` | `max_subsequence_ratio`, `min_align_ratio`, `min_hit_length`, `deduplicate_sequences`, `max_hits`, `max_template_date` | Hit selection criteria |

At the `DataPipelineConfig` level, the two database paths that govern template search are `seqres_database_path` (the FASTA file of PDB chain sequences that hmmsearch queries against) and `pdb_database_path` (the directory or TAR archive of mmCIF files that StructureStore reads from).

Sources: [msa_config.py](/src/alphafold3/data/msa_config.py#L133-L200), [pipeline.py](/src/alphafold3/data/pipeline.py#L213-L301)

## What Comes Next

After template search completes, the resulting `TemplateFeatures` are merged with MSA features and passed into the featurisation and batching stage, which prepares the final NumPy arrays for the neural network. To understand how template features are assembled into model inputs, see [Featurisation and Batching](10-featurisation-and-batching). For the MSA construction that precedes template search, see [MSA Search Pipeline](8-msa-search-pipeline).

# Featurisation and Batching



The featurisation and batching stage is the critical bridge between AlphaFold 3's search pipelines and its neural network core. It transforms raw MSA hits, template structures, and input sequences into a **padded, bucketed tensor batch** (`BatchDict`) that the Evoformer and Diffusion modules consume directly. Understanding this pipeline is essential for diagnosing shape mismatches, compilation overhead, and feature-level bugs.

## Architectural Overview

The featurisation pipeline follows a strict layered architecture: **validation → tokenization → per-feature computation → bucket-based padding → batch assembly → NaN check**. Each layer is stateless and deterministic for a given random seed, enabling reproducible inference across runs.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["folding_input.Input<br/>(JSON → chains, MSA, templates)"] --> B["validate_fold_input()"]
    B --> C{"For each rng_seed"}
    C --> D["WholePdbPipeline.process_item()"]
    D --> E["to_structure() +<br/>extract MSA/template maps"]
    E --> F["process_structure()"]
    F --> G["Structure Cleaning"]
    G --> H["Inter-chain Bond Extraction"]
    H --> I["Flat Atom Layout Creation"]
    I --> J["Tokenizer<br/>(atoms → tokens)"]
    J --> K["calculate_bucket_size()"]
    K --> L["PaddingShapes"]
    L --> M["Feature Computation Fan-out"]
    M --> M1["MSA.compute_features()"]
    M --> M2["Templates.compute_features()"]
    M --> M3["TokenFeatures.compute_features()"]
    M --> M4["RefStructure.compute_features()"]
    M --> M5["AtomCrossAtt.compute_features()"]
    M --> M6["Frames.compute_features()"]
    M --> M7["PseudoBetaInfo.compute_features()"]
    M --> M8["PolymerLigandBondInfo"]
    M --> M9["LigandLigandBondInfo"]
    M --> M10["ConvertModelOutput"]
    M --> M11["PredictedStructureInfo"]
    M1 & M2 & M3 & M4 & M5 & M6 & M7 & M8 & M9 & M10 & M11 --> N["Batch Assembly<br/>(feat_batch.Batch)"]
    N --> O["as_data_dict()"]
    O --> P["NaN Check"]
    P --> Q["BatchDict"]
```

Sources: [featurisation.py](src/alphafold3/data/featurisation.py#L47-L121), [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/model/pipeline/pipeline.py#L86-L438)

## Entry Point: `featurise_input()`

The public API for featurisation is [`featurise_input()`](src/alphafold3/data/featurisation.py#L47), which takes a validated `folding_input.Input`, a CCD object, and optional bucket sizes, then returns a `Sequence[BatchDict]` — one batch per `rng_seed`. The function first validates that all protein chains carry unpaired MSA, paired MSA, and templates, and that all RNA chains carry at least unpaired MSA. It then instantiates a `WholePdbPipeline` with the provided configuration and processes each seed independently, producing a fully materialized NumPy batch per seed.

Key configuration parameters passed through to the pipeline include `buckets` (for JAX compilation control), `resolve_msa_overlaps` (deduplication of unpaired against paired MSA), `fix_standalone_glycans` (training-matching behavior for glycan leaving atoms), and `conformer_max_iterations` (RDKit conformer search budget).

Sources: [featurisation.py](src/alphafold3/data/featurisation.py#L33-L121)

## Tokenization: From Atoms to Evoformer Tokens

The **tokenizer** is the central mapping that determines how atomic representations collapse into the token grid that the Evoformer operates on. This is not a simple residue-level mapping — it is a **polymorphic tokenizer** whose behavior depends on chain type and residue standardness.

| Chain Type | Standard Residue | Token Granularity | Representative Atom |
|---|---|---|---|
| Protein | Standard (e.g. ALA) | 1 token per residue | CA |
| Protein | Non-standard + MSE | 1 token per residue | CA |
| Protein | Non-standard (other) | 1 token per atom | Each atom |
| RNA/DNA | Standard (e.g. A, DA) | 1 token per residue | C1' |
| RNA/DNA | Non-standard | 1 token per atom | Each atom |
| Ligand (non-polymer) | N/A | 1 token per atom | Each atom |

The tokenizer produces three outputs: **`all_tokens`** (an `AtomLayout` with one representative atom per token), **`all_token_atoms_layout`** (an `AtomLayout` with shape `(num_tokens, max_atoms_per_token)` listing all atoms per token), and **`standard_token_idxs`** (a mapping used to align MSA/template columns to the potentially-expanded token grid). The `max_atoms_per_token` defaults to **24**, accommodating the largest standard residue atom count from the CCD.

> [!TIP]
> Non-standard polymer residues are "flattened" into one-token-per-atom mode when `flatten_non_standard_residues=True` (the default). This means a modified residue like SEP (phosphoserine) generates 12+ tokens instead of 1, significantly inflating the token count and bucket size. For large complexes with many modifications, this can trigger JAX recompilation if bucket sizes aren't pre-configured.

Sources: [features.py](src/alphafold3/model/features.py#L173-L408)

## Bucket-Based Padding and Compilation Control

JAX compiles a separate XLA program for each distinct input shape. To prevent excessive recompilation, AlphaFold 3 uses a **bucketing scheme** that pads all inputs to a predetermined set of token counts. The `calculate_bucket_size()` function uses binary search (`bisect_left`) to find the smallest bucket ≥ the actual token count.

```python
# Default bucket behavior: no pre-defined buckets → pad to exact token count
buckets = None  # → padded_token_length = num_tokens

# Pre-defined buckets: pad to next bucket, avoiding recompilation
buckets = [256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096]  # → e.g. 300 tokens → pad to 512
```

If the token count exceeds the largest bucket, a warning is logged and the token count itself is used as the bucket size — which **will trigger recompilation**. The padding shapes are then derived from the bucket size:

| Padding Dimension | Calculation |
|---|---|
| `num_tokens` | `padded_token_length` (from bucket) |
| `msa_size` | `msa_crop_size` (default 16384) |
| `num_chains` | `pad_num_chains` (default 1000) |
| `num_templates` | `max_templates` (default 4) |
| `num_atoms` | `padded_token_length × average_num_atoms_per_token`, rounded up to `atom_cross_att_queries_subset_size` (default 32) |

Sources: [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/model/pipeline/pipeline.py#L43-L71), [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/model/pipeline/pipeline.py#L279-L292)

## Feature Computation: The Eleven Feature Groups

The `Batch` dataclass assembles exactly **eleven feature groups**, each a frozen dataclass with its own `compute_features()` classmethod. Every group independently pads its output to the `PaddingShapes` dimensions before returning.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Input Data"
        A["MSA (A3M strings)"]
        B["Templates (mmCIFs)"]
        C["Structure + CCD"]
    end
    subgraph "Feature Groups → Batch"
        D["MSA"]
        E["Templates"]
        F["TokenFeatures"]
        G["RefStructure"]
        H["AtomCrossAtt"]
        I["Frames"]
        J["PseudoBetaInfo"]
        K["PolymerLigandBondInfo"]
        L["LigandLigandBondInfo"]
        M["ConvertModelOutput"]
        N["PredictedStructureInfo"]
    end
    A --> D
    B --> E
    C --> F & G & H & I & J & K & L & M & N
    D & E & F & G & H & I & J & K & L & M & N --> O["feat_batch.Batch"]
```

### MSA Features

The `MSA` feature group is the most complex, performing **per-chain featurization → cross-chain pairing → cropping → merging → padding**. For each chain, the unpaired A3M is parsed into an `Msa` object and featurized (producing `msa`, `deletion_matrix` arrays). Paired MSA is featurized separately and suffixed with `_all_seq`. Profile features (per-position residue frequency) and deletion means are computed via `data3.get_profile_features()`.

When multiple unique protein chains exist (detected via `num_unique_chains > 1`), **MSA pairing** is activated: `msa_pairing.create_paired_features()` pairs sequences across chains by species taxonomy, limited by `max_paired_sequence_per_species` (default 600). Paired sequences are then deduplicated against unpaired sequences if `resolve_msa_overlaps=True`.

MSA cropping uses `choose_paired_unpaired_msa_crop_sizes()` to allocate the total `msa_crop_size` budget (default 16384) between paired and unpaired rows, with a 50% cap on paired rows. After merging chains via `merge_msa_features()` and `merge_paired_and_unpaired_msa()`, the MSA is cropped to standard token indices and padded.

| MSA Field | Shape | dtype | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `msa` | `(msa_size, num_tokens)` | int8 | Residue types per MSA row/column |
| `msa_mask` | `(msa_size, num_tokens)` | bool | Valid MSA entries |
| `deletion_matrix` | `(msa_size, num_tokens)` | int8 | Deletion counts (clipped) |
| `profile` | `(num_tokens, num_residue_types)` | float32 | Position-wise residue frequency |
| `deletion_mean` | `(num_tokens,)` | float32 | Mean deletions per position |
| `num_alignments` | scalar | int32 | Actual MSA depth before padding |

Sources: [features.py](src/alphafold3/model/features.py#L411-L715)

### Template Features

Template features are computed per protein chain by parsing each template's mmCIF, extracting polymer features via `templates.get_polymer_features()` (which realigns template residues to the query), and packaging them with `package_template_features()`. Templates are reduced to `max_templates` (default 4) per chain, then concatenated across chains on the token dimension. Like MSA, template columns are indexed by `standard_token_idxs` to handle non-standard residue expansion.

| Template Field | Shape | dtype |
|---|---|---|
| `template_aatype` | `(num_templates, num_tokens)` | int32 |
| `template_atom_positions` | `(num_templates, num_tokens, 24, 3)` | float32 |
| `template_atom_mask` | `(num_templates, num_tokens, 24)` | bool |

Sources: [features.py](src/alphafold3/model/features.py#L718-L883)

### Token Features

`TokenFeatures` encodes per-token identity and topology: residue type (`aatype`), position indices (`residue_index`, `token_index`), chain symmetry identifiers (`asym_id`, `entity_id`, `sym_id`), and chain-type boolean flags (`is_protein`, `is_rna`, `is_dna`, `is_ligand`, `is_nonstandard_polymer_chain`, `is_water`). The symmetry identifiers follow the convention where identical sequences share an `entity_id` but receive distinct `asym_id` and incrementing `sym_id` values.

Sources: [features.py](src/alphafold3/model/features.py#L904-L997)

### Reference Structure and Frames

`RefStructure` generates 3D reference coordinates for each atom in the `all_token_atoms_layout`. For standard polymer residues, these come from ideal CCD coordinates. For ligands, RDKit conformer generation is attempted (with a fallback to CCD model coordinates if `ref_max_modified_date` allows). A **deterministic** reference structure is also computed with a fixed seed (`12312837`) for frame construction when `deterministic_frames=True`.

`Frames` builds local coordinate frames (origin + 3 orthonormal axes) per token from the reference structure, which the Diffusion Head uses to define noise in a rotation-invariant local frame.

Sources: [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/model/pipeline/pipeline.py#L360-L421)

## The Batch Object: Final Assembly and Validation

After all eleven feature groups are computed, they are assembled into a single `feat_batch.Batch` frozen dataclass. This object is registered as a JAX pytree via `jax.tree_util.register_dataclass`, enabling seamless `jax.jit` compilation. The `Batch` exposes:

- **`as_data_dict()`** → flattens all feature groups into a single `dict[str, np.ndarray]` (`BatchDict`) for model consumption
- **`from_data_dict()`** → reconstructs the structured `Batch` from a flat dictionary
- **`num_res`** property → returns `token_features.aatype.shape[-1]`

The final step in `process_item()` is a **NaN check**: every numeric field in the `BatchDict` is summed and tested for NaN, raising `NanDataError` if any is found. This catches upstream issues (e.g., failed conformer generation producing NaN coordinates) before they propagate into the model.

> [!TIP]
> The `Batch` object is a JAX pytree, meaning `jax.jit`-compiled functions can accept it directly as an argument. However, the model's forward pass actually consumes the flattened `BatchDict` (via `as_data_dict()`), not the structured `Batch`. The pytree registration primarily benefits checkpoint serialization and `jax.grad` traversal over batch elements.

Sources: [feat_batch.py](src/alphafold3/model/feat_batch.py#L28-L93), [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/model/pipeline/pipeline.py#L423-L482)

## WholePdbPipeline Configuration Reference

The `WholePdbPipeline.Config` controls all aspects of featurisation and batching. The table below lists every configurable parameter with its default and purpose.

| Parameter | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `max_atoms_per_token` | 24 | Atom slots per token (dense atom representation width) |
| `pad_num_chains` | 1000 | Padding for chain-count dimensions |
| `buckets` | None | Bucket sizes for padding (None = no bucketing) |
| `max_total_residues` | None | Reject inputs exceeding this token count |
| `min_total_residues` | None | Reject inputs below this token count |
| `msa_crop_size` | 16384 | Maximum MSA depth across all chains |
| `max_template_date` | None | Cutoff date for template inclusion |
| `ref_max_modified_date` | None | CCD fallback date for conformer generation |
| `max_templates` | 4 | Maximum template structures per chain |
| `max_paired_sequence_per_species` | 600 | MSA pairing limit per taxonomic species |
| `drop_ligand_leaving_atoms` | True | Remove leaving atoms from ligand CCD entries |
| `average_num_atoms_per_token` | 24 | Expected atoms/token for atom count padding |
| `atom_cross_att_queries_subset_size` | 32 | Query subset size for atom cross attention |
| `atom_cross_att_keys_subset_size` | 128 | Key subset size for atom cross attention |
| `flatten_non_standard_residues` | True | Expand non-standard residues to 1-token-per-atom |
| `deterministic_frames` | True | Use fixed-seed reference positions for frames |
| `conformer_max_iterations` | None | Override RDKit conformer search iterations |
| `resolve_msa_overlaps` | True | Deduplicate unpaired MSA against paired MSA |
| `fix_standalone_glycans` | False | Keep glycan leaving atoms even if unbonded |

Sources: [pipeline.py](src/alphafold3/model/pipeline/pipeline.py#L89-L159)

## Data Flow: From Search Results to Batch

The featurisation pipeline receives its MSA and template data from the [MSA Search Pipeline](8-msa-search-pipeline) and [Template Search](9-template-search) stages. The `process_item()` method on `WholePdbPipeline` extracts these from the `folding_input.Input` object by iterating over chains: `ProteinChain` instances contribute unpaired MSA, paired MSA, and templates; `RnaChain` instances contribute only unpaired MSA. All other chain types (DNA, ligands) contribute no evolutionary information but are fully represented in the token and structural features.

The resulting `BatchDict` flows directly into the [Evoformer Trunk](11-evoformer-trunk), which consumes MSA rows, template features, and token features to produce pairwise representations, and subsequently into the [Diffusion Head](12-diffusion-head) and [Atom Cross Attention](13-atom-cross-attention) modules, which consume the reference structure, frames, and atom cross-attention features to denoise atomic coordinates.


# Evoformer Trunk



The **Evoformer Trunk** is the representational backbone of AlphaFold 3 — the module that transforms raw input features (MSA, templates, bonds, relative positions) into the **single embeddings** and **pair embeddings** that drive every downstream prediction head. Unlike AlphaFold 2's monolithic Evoformer stack, AlphaFold 3 decomposes its trunk into two distinct phases: an **MSA-aware Evoformer stack** that jointly evolves MSA and pair representations, followed by a **Pairformer stack** that refines pair and single representations without MSA. This two-phase architecture is the key structural innovation enabling AlphaFold 3's generalised input space (proteins, RNA, DNA, ligands, ions, covalent bonds) while remaining computationally tractable.

Sources: [evoformer.py](src/alphafold3/model/network/evoformer.py#L39-L84), [model.py](src/alphafold3/model/model.py#L280-L319)

## Architecture Overview

The Evoformer Trunk executes a strict sequential pipeline. Each phase enriches the pair representation before handing it to the next, and only the final Pairformer phase produces the single representation consumed by downstream heads.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Phase0["Target Feature Embedding"]
        TF1["Token One-Hot + MSA Profile + Deletion Mean"]
        TF2["Per-Atom Conditioning (AtomCrossAtt)"]
        TF["target_feat = concat(TF1, TF2)"]
        TF1 --> TF
        TF2 --> TF
    end

    subgraph Phase1["Pair Initialisation"]
        PE["Seq-Pair Embedding (left_single + right_single)"]
        PV["Previous-Cycle Pair Embedding (LayerNorm → Linear)"]
        RE["Relative Position Encoding"]
        BE["Bond Embedding"]
        TE["Template Pair Embedding"]
        PE --> PV --> RE --> BE --> TE
    end

    subgraph Phase2["MSA Stack (EvoformerIteration × N)"]
        MSAMSK["MSA Shuffle → Truncate → Featurise"]
        EVO["EvoformerIteration × num_layer"]
        MSAMSK --> EVO
    end

    subgraph Phase3["Single Initialisation"]
        SI["Linear(target_feat)"]
        SPV["Previous-Cycle Single Embedding"]
    end

    subgraph Phase4["Pairformer Stack (PairFormerIteration × 48)"]
        PF["PairFormerIteration (with_single=True) × 48"]
    end

    TF --> PE
    TE --> MSAMSK
    EVO --> SI
    SPV --> PF

    OUT["Output: {single, pair, target_feat}"]
    PF --> OUT
```

The full `__call__` method enforces this ordering: pair embedding → previous-cycle injection → relative encoding → bond embedding → template embedding → MSA stack → single embedding → previous-cycle single injection → Pairformer stack. This is not merely a convention — the `del key` statement after the MSA phase signals that all stochastic processing is complete before the deterministic Pairformer begins.

Sources: [evoformer.py](src/alphafold3/model/network/evoformer.py#L252-L356)

## Channel and Layer Configuration

The default configuration establishes the dimensional contract that all downstream heads rely upon:

| Parameter | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `msa_channel` | 64 | Width of MSA activations within the Evoformer stack |
| `seq_channel` | 384 | Width of the single (per-token) representation |
| `pair_channel` | 128 | Width of the pair (token×token) representation |
| `num_msa` | 1024 | Maximum MSA rows fed into the Evoformer stack |
| `max_relative_idx` | 32 | Clipping range for relative residue/token index encoding |
| `max_relative_chain` | 2 | Clipping range for relative chain index encoding |
| `pairformer.num_layer` | 48 | Number of PairFormer iterations in the trunk stack |
| `msa_stack.num_layer` | 4 (default) | Number of Evoformer iterations in the MSA stack |

The **48-layer Pairformer** is the dominant computational phase. Its configuration is a `PairformerConfig` that extends `PairFormerIteration.Config` with rematerialisation controls (`block_remat`, `remat_block_size`) for memory-efficient backpropagation through the deep stack.
